I say: Many of the later scholars among the followers of the imams have erred regarding their imams because of this. The imams were scrupulous about using the term "tahrim" (prohibition) and used the term "karahah" (disliking) instead. Then the later scholars denied prohibition regarding what the imams had described as disliked. Then the term "karahah" became easy for them and its burden light, so some of them understood it as reprehensible but not prohibited (tanzih), and others extended it to mean "leaving the better course" (karahat tark al-awla). This is very frequent in their usage, and because of it a great error has occurred regarding the Sharia and regarding the imams.

Imam Ahmad said regarding combining two sisters by ownership of the right hand: "I dislike it, and I do not say it is haram," although his school holds it to be prohibited. He was scrupulous only about using the term "tahrim," on account of the saying of Uthman.

Abu al-Qasim al-Khiraqi said, in what he related from Abu Abd Allah (Ahmad): "It is disliked to perform wudu' in vessels of gold and silver," although his school holds that it is not permissible. In the narration of Abu Dawud he said: "It is recommended not to enter the bath except with a loincloth," and this is a recommendation of obligation. In the narration of Ishaq ibn Mansur he said: "If most of a man's wealth is haram, I do not like that his wealth be eaten," and this is by way of prohibition.

In the narration of his son Abd Allah he said: "I do not like the eating of what is slaughtered for the planets, nor for the stars, nor for the church, and everything slaughtered for other than Allah." Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Prohibited to you are carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that which has been dedicated to other than Allah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3].

Consider how he said, "I do not like," regarding what Allah, glorified is He, has explicitly prohibited, and he himself argued from Allah's prohibition of it in His Book. He said in the narration of al-Athram: "I dislike the flesh and milk of the jallalah (an animal that feeds on filth)," and he clearly stated the prohibition in the narration of Harb and others. He said in the narration of his son Abd Allah: "I dislike eating the flesh of the snake and the scorpion, because the snake has fangs and the scorpion has a sting," and his school does not differ on its prohibition. He said in the narration of Harb: "If a dog hunts without being sent, I do not like it, because the Prophet ﷺ said: 'When you send your dog and say the name of Allah.'" Thus he applied the phrase "I do not like" to what is haram in his view.

Then Ibn al-Qayyim said:

The Salaf used the term karahah in the meaning in which it is used in the words of Allah and His Messenger. But the later scholars agreed to restrict karahah to what is not prohibited but whose abandonment is preferable to its performance. Then whoever among them understood the words of the imams in accordance with this newly coined terminology erred in that. And a graver error than this is that of whoever understood the term karahah or the term "la yanbaghi" (it is not fitting) in the words of Allah and His Messenger according to this newly invented technical meaning. The usage of "la yanbaghi" in the words of Allah and His Messenger is consistent for what is forbidden by the Sharia and by decree, and for what is impossible and inconceivable, as in His saying: ﴿And it is not befitting for the Most Merciful to take a son﴾ [Maryam: 92], and His saying: ﴿And We did not teach him poetry, nor is it befitting for him﴾ [Ya-Sin: 69], and His saying: ﴿And the devils did not bring it down, nor is it befitting for them﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 210-211].

And His saying on the tongue of His Prophet: "The son of Adam denied Me, and it is not befitting for him; the son of Adam reviled Me, and it is not befitting for him." And his ﷺ saying: "Indeed Allah does not sleep, and it is not befitting for Him to sleep." And his ﷺ saying about silk garments: "This is not befitting for the righteous (al-muttaqin)," and similar examples.

[Section: the arguments of those who reject analogy]

We have presented sections of benefit and comprehensive principles in establishing qiyas (analogical reasoning) and arguing with it, which you may not find in any other book, nor anything close to them. So let us now mention, alongside them, the texts and evidences opposed to them, which indicate the condemnation of qiyas, that it is not part of religion, and that one can dispense with it and be content with the two revelations. Here we present them in detail and clarity, by the praise of Allah.

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿O you who have believed, obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you. And if you dispute over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger, if you should believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾ [al-Nisa': 59]. The Muslims agreed that referring to Allah, glorified is He, is referring to His Book, and referring to the Messenger ﷺ is referring to him in his presence and life, and to his Sunnah in his absence and after his death. Qiyas is neither this nor that.

It cannot be said that referring to qiyas is referring to Allah and His Messenger, because the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger ('alayhi al-salam) indicate it, as previously established. For Allah, glorified is He, only referred us to His Book and the Sunnah of His Messenger, and never referred us to the analogies of our minds and opinions. Rather, He, the Exalted, said to His Prophet ﷺ: ﴿And judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 49], and He said: ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you the Book in truth, that you may judge between people by what Allah has shown you﴾ [al-Nisa': 105]. He did not say "by what you see." And He said: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, those are the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 44], ﴿...those are the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 45], ﴿...those are the defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 47]. And the Exalted said: ﴿Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾ [al-A'raf: 3]. And the Exalted said: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as clarification for all things﴾ [al-Nahl: 89]. And He said: ﴿Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book, recited to them? Indeed in that is mercy and reminder for a people who believe﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 51]. And He said: ﴿Say: If I go astray, I only go astray against myself; and if I am guided, it is by what my Lord reveals to me﴾ [Saba': 50]. So if qiyas were guidance, guidance would not be confined to revelation.

And He said: ﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge in what they dispute among themselves﴾ [al-Nisa': 65]. Thus He negated faith until His judgement alone is found, which is His judgement during his life, and the judgement of his Sunnah alone after his death. And the Exalted said: ﴿O you who have believed, do not put yourselves forward before Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Hujurat: 1], meaning: do not speak until he speaks.

The opponents of qiyas said: To report about Allah that He prohibited what He was silent about, or obligated it, by analogy to what He spoke of prohibiting or obligating, is a putting forward before Him. For if one says, "I have prohibited you usury in wheat," and we reply, "We also analogize acorns to your words," this is plain putting forward.

They said: Allah, glorified is He, has prohibited us from saying about Him what we do not know. So if we do that, we have certainly committed this prohibited act, for we do not know that He intended by prohibiting usury in gold and silver the prohibition of it in dried meat. This is a pursuing from us of what we have no knowledge of, and a transgression of what has been set as limits for us. "Whoever transgresses the limits of Allah has wronged himself." The obligation is to stop at His limits, neither exceeding them nor falling short of them.

It cannot be said: Then the invalidation of qiyas, its prohibition, and the prohibition against it is itself a putting forward before Allah and His Messenger, and a prohibition of what He did not explicitly prohibit, and a pursuing from you of what you have no knowledge of. Because we say: Allah, glorified and exalted is He, brought us out of our mothers' wombs knowing nothing, sent down His Book to us, and sent His Messenger to us to teach us the Book and the wisdom. So what we know and what he has made clear to us is from the religion, and what he has not taught us, nor made clear to us that it is from the religion, is not from the religion by necessity. And everything that is not from the religion is false. "There is nothing after the truth but error." And Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3]. So what Allah, glorified is He, has perfected and made clear is our religion, and we have no religion other than it. Where, then, in what He has perfected for us is the saying: "Analogize what I have been silent about to what I have spoken of in obligating, prohibiting, or permitting, whether the common factor between them is a cause, an indication of a cause, or an resembling attribute. So employ all of that, attribute it to me, to my Messenger, and to my religion, and judge by it over me"?

They said: And Allah, glorified is He, has informed: ﴿Indeed, assumption avails nothing against the truth﴾ [Yunus: 36]. And His Messenger informed: "Indeed, assumption is the most false of speech," and forbade it. And among the greatest assumption is the assumption of the analogists, for they are not certain that Allah, glorified and exalted is He, prohibited the sale of sesame for sesame oil, or of sweets for grapes, or of starch for wheat. Rather these are merely bare assumptions that avail nothing against the truth.

They said: And if the analogy of the fart to "al-salamu 'alaykum" is not from the assumption that we were forbidden to follow and to judge by, and that He informed us avails nothing against the truth, then there is no false assumption in the world. Where is the fart from "al-salamu 'alaykum"? And if the analogy of water that has touched the pure and good limbs, which are pure and good in the sight of Allah, in removing ritual impurity, to water that has touched the most filthy excrements, carrion, and impurities, is not an assumption, then we do not know what assumption Allah, glorified is He, forbade speaking by and condemned in His Book and stripped of truth. And if the analogy of the enemies of Allah and His Messenger, the worshippers of crosses and the Jews, who are the strongest of people in enmity toward the believers, to His friends, the best of His creation, the masters of the community, its scholars and righteous, in the equality of their blood and the application of retaliation between them, is not an assumption, then there is no assumption in the world whose following is condemned.

They said: And it is strange that you analogized the enemies of Allah to His friends in the application of retaliation between them, so you killed a thousand friends of Allah who had killed one Christian who openly reviled Allah, His Messenger and His Book; yet you did not analogize one who struck a man's head with a mace, scattering his brains before him, to one who stabbed him with a needle and killed him.

They said: And we will show you from the contradiction of your analogies, their disagreement, and the severity of their confusion, what shows that they are from other than Allah.

They said: Allah, the Exalted, did not entrust the explanation of His Sharia to our opinions, analogies, and deductions. Rather He entrusted it to His Messenger, who explains it on His behalf. So what he explained must be followed, and what he did not explain is not from the religion. And we beseech you by Allah: Is your reliance in these resembling analogies and estimated, conjectural attributes upon the explanation of the Messenger, or upon the opinions, assumptions, and conjectures of men? Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Reminder, that you may explain to the people what has been sent down to them﴾ [al-Nahl: 44]. So where did the Prophet ﷺ explain that if I prohibit something, or obligate it, or permit it, you should extract a resembling attribute that unites that with all that I have been silent about, and attach it to that and analogize upon it?

They said: Allah, Exalted is He, has forbidden striking similitudes for Him, so just as similitudes may not be struck for Him, they may not be struck for His religion. And to derive the ruling on what He did not specify from what He did specify, because of the resemblance between them, is a case of striking similitudes for His religion. This is different from what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) struck as similitudes in many of the rulings about which he was asked. For example, when he commanded them to make up the prayer they had missed while sleeping, they said: "Should we not pray it at its proper time tomorrow?" He said: "Does he who forbids you usury accept it from you?" Likewise, when Umar asked him about kissing for one who is fasting, he said: "Tell me, if you rinsed your mouth with water and then spat it out?" Likewise, he said to a woman who asked him about performing Hajj on behalf of her father: "Tell me, if your father had a debt?" Likewise, he said to one who asked whether he is rewarded for having intercourse with his wife: "Tell me, if he had placed it in the unlawful?"

[Among the similitudes which Allah and His Messenger struck]

Among the finest of these similitudes, the most eloquent, and the greatest in bringing things close to understanding, is what Imam Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi narrated from the hadith of al-Harith al-Ash'ari, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah, Glorified is He, commanded Yahya ibn Zakariyya (John the son of Zachariah) with five words, to act upon them and to command the Children of Israel to act upon them. He was about to delay in doing so, so Isa said: 'Indeed Allah has commanded you with five words, that you act upon them and command the Children of Israel to act upon them. Either you command them, or I will command them.' Yahya said: 'I fear that if you precede me, I will be swallowed up by the earth or punished.' So he gathered the people in Bayt al-Maqdis, and the mosque filled up, and they sat on the ledges. He said: 'Indeed Allah has commanded me with five words, that I act upon them and that I command you to act upon them. The first of them: that you worship Allah and do not associate anything with Him. Indeed the example of one who associates others with Allah is like the example of a man who bought a slave from his pure wealth with gold or silver, and said: "This is my house and this is my work, so work and pay me." The slave would work and pay someone other than his master. Which of you would be pleased for his slave to be like that? Indeed Allah has commanded you to pray. When you pray, do not turn about, for indeed Allah directs His face toward the face of His servant during his prayer as long as he does not turn. He has commanded you to fast, and the example of that is like the example of a man in a company, with him a bag containing musk, and all of them are pleased by its fragrance. Indeed the breath of one who is fasting is more fragrant with Allah than the scent of musk. He has commanded you to give charity, and the example of that is like the example of a man whom the enemy captured, bound his hands to his neck, and brought forward to strike his neck. He said: "I will ransom myself from you with everything, little or much," and he ransomed himself from them. He has commanded you to remember Allah, and the example of that is like the example of a man whom the enemy pursued swiftly, until he came to a strong fortress and secured himself from them. Likewise, the servant cannot secure himself from Satan except by the remembrance of Allah.'" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "And I command you with five which Allah has commanded me: listening, obedience, jihad, emigration, and the community. Indeed whoever separates from the community by a span has indeed removed the rope of Islam from his neck, unless he returns. Whoever calls to the calls of the Jahiliyyah, he is among the kneeling of Hell." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, even if he prays and fasts?" He said: "Even if he prays and fasts. So call with the call of Allah which named you Muslims, believers, servants of Allah." This is a sound hadith.

In the Sahihayn (the two Sahih collections) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah: that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Tell me, if there were a river at the door of one of you, in which he bathed five times a day, would any of its dirt remain on him?" They said: "No." He said: "That is the example of the five prayers, by which Allah erases sins." The Prophet (ﷺ) likened the believer who recites the Qur'an to the citron (utrujjah) in the goodness of its taste and fragrance, and its opposite to the colocynth (handhalah). He likened the believer who does not recite to the date in the goodness of its taste and its lack of fragrance, and the wicked one who recites to the basil (raihanah), whose fragrance is pleasant and whose taste is bitter. He likened the believer to a green stalk of grain which the winds never stop bending, and the believer is always afflicted by calamity. He likened the hypocrite to the cedar tree (ar-arz, which is the pine), which does not sway or bend until it is cut down all at once. He likened the believer to the palm tree in the abundance of its goodness and benefits, the people's need for it, and their coming and going to it for their benefit. He compared his community to rain, for the benefit of its beginning and its end, and the life of existence by it. He likened his community and the two earlier scriptural communities, in what Allah singled out for his community and honored it with, to laborers who worked for a specified wage from a man for a day, on the condition that he would pay them their wages. But they did not complete the rest of their day and abandoned work in the middle of the day. So his community worked the rest of the day, and they completed the reward of both groups. Jibril and Mika'il struck for him and his community the example of a king who acquired a house, then built a dwelling within it, then made a feast, then sent a messenger calling the people to his food. Some of them answered the messenger and some left him. Allah is the King, Muhammad is the Messenger who calls, the house is Islam, and the dwelling is Paradise. Whoever answers him enters Islam, and whoever enters Islam enters the house of the King and eats from it. Whoever does not answer him does not enter his house and does not eat from it.

And in the Musnad and al-Tirmidhi, from the hadith of al-Nawwas ibn Sam'an, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah struck a parable: a straight path. On either side of the path are two walls with open doors, and over the doors are hanging curtains. At the entrance to the path is a caller who says: 'O people, enter the path all together and do not deviate.' And a caller calls from above the path. Whenever a person wants to open one of those doors, he says: 'Woe to you, do not open it, for if you open it you will enter it.' So the path is Islam, the two walls are the limits of Allah, the open doors are the prohibitions of Allah. No one falls into a limit of the limits of Allah until he uncovers the curtain. The caller at the head of the path is the Book of Allah, and the caller from above the path is the admonisher of Allah in the heart of every Muslim." So let the one who knows consider the worth of this parable, let him reflect upon it with true reflection, weigh himself by it, and look at where he stands in relation to it. And success is from Allah.

He also said: "My similitude and the similitude of the prophets before me is like the example of a man who built a house, completed it and beautified it, except for the place of one brick. People began to enter it and marvel at it, saying: 'If only the place of that brick were filled.' So I am the place of that brick." Narrated by Muslim.

In the Sahihayn from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah and Abu Sa'id, from him (ﷺ): "My similitude and the similitude of my community is like the example of a man who kindled a fire, and the creatures and moths began to fall into it, while I am taking hold of your waists away from the fire, and you are plunging into it." He also likened the one who falls into doubtful matters to a shepherd who grazes around the sanctuary, about to fall into it.

Al-Hafiz Abu Muhammad ibn Khallad al-Ramahurmuzi said: Abu Sa'id al-Harrani narrated to us, Yahya ibn Abdullah al-Babultti narrated to us, Safwan ibn Amr narrated to us, who said: Sulaym ibn Amir narrated to me, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I was aided with awe for a distance of a month's journey, I was given comprehensive words (jawami' al-kalim), I was given wisdom, and similitudes of the Qur'an were struck for me. While I was sleeping, two angels came to me, one stood at my head and the other stood at my feet. The one at my head said to the one at my feet: 'Strike a similitude, and I will explain it.' The one at my head said, inclining toward me: 'Let your eye sleep, let your ear listen, and let your heart understand.' So I was in that state: the ear hears, the heart understands, and the eye sleeps. He said: Then he struck a similitude and said: 'A pool in which there is a firmly rooted tree, and on the tree there is a protruding branch. A striker came and struck the tree, and the branch fell, and with it fell much foliage, all of it into the pool, not exceeding it. Then he struck a second time, and much foliage fell, all of it into the pool, not exceeding it. Then he struck a third time, and much foliage fell, and I do not know what fell into it more, or what came out of it.'" He said: Then the one at my feet explained, and said: "As for the pool, it is Paradise. As for the tree, it is the community. As for the branch, it is the Prophet (ﷺ). As for the striker, he is the Angel of Death. He struck the first blow in the first generation, and the Prophet (ﷺ) and the people of his era fell. He struck the second blow in the second generation, and all of that fell into Paradise. Then he struck the third blow in the third generation, and I do not know what fell into it more, or what came out of it."

In the Musnad, from the hadith of Jabir: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) delivered a sermon, his eyes reddened, his voice rose, and his anger intensified, until he seemed like a warner of an army, saying: 'The enemy has come upon you in the morning and in the evening.' Then he would say: 'I was sent, and the Hour is like these two,' and he would join his index finger and middle finger."

And in the hadith of al-Mustawrid: "I was sent in the breath of the Hour, I preceded it just as this has preceded this," and he pointed with his two fingers. And in the Musnad from him: "Indeed my similitude and the similitude of what Allah sent me with is like the example of a man who came to his people and said: 'O my people, indeed I have seen the army with my own eyes, and I am the naked warner, so flee for safety!' A group of them obeyed him, departed in the night at their leisure, and were saved. Another group denied him, remained where they were in the morning, and the army attacked them in the morning, destroyed them and wiped them out. Likewise is the example of him who obeys me and follows what I have brought, and the example of him who disobeys me and denies what I have brought of the truth." And in the Sahihayn from him: "My similitude and the similitude of what Allah sent me with of guidance and knowledge is like the example of abundant rain that fell upon a land. A part of it accepted the water and produced grass and abundant herbage. Some of it was barren ground which held water, and Allah benefited people by it, so they drank, watered their livestock, and cultivated. It also fell upon another part, which was only smooth flat land that holds no water and produces no grass. That is the example of one who acquires understanding of the religion of Allah and benefits from what Allah sent me with, so he knows and teaches. And the example of one who does not lift his head toward that and does not accept the guidance of Allah with which I was sent."

In the Sahihayn, from him (ﷺ), that he addressed the people and said: "By Allah, it is not poverty that I fear for you, but I fear for you what Allah brings forth for you of the splendor of this world." A man said: "O Messenger of Allah, does good bring evil?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) remained silent, then said: "How did you say that?" He said: "O Messenger of Allah, does good bring evil?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed good brings only good. Among what spring produces is that which kills or causes bloating, except the grazing animal that eats the greenery until its flanks become distended, then it faces the sun, releases dung and urine, then chews its cud and returns to eating. Whoever takes wealth by its right, it will be blessed for him, and whoever takes wealth without its right, his example is like one who eats and is never satisfied."

Maymunah said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Amr ibn al-As: 'The world is green and sweet. Whoever fears Allah regarding it and does right, well; otherwise he is like one who eats and is never satisfied. Between people in this matter is like the distance between two stars, one rising in the east and the other setting in the west.'" And he (ﷺ) likened himself in this world to a rider who passed through a barren land, saw a tree, took shade under it, then departed and left it."

And in the Musnad and al-Tirmidhi from him: "The world in comparison to the Hereafter is nothing but what one of you dips his finger into the sea; let him look at what it returns with." And he passed with the Companions by a dead young goat, and said: "Do you see this, how it was cast aside by its people? By Him in whose hand is my soul, the world is more insignificant to Allah than this is to its people."

He said: "My example, your example, and the example of this world are like a people who traversed a barren desert, not knowing how much of it they had crossed or how much remained. Their backs grew weary, their provisions ran out, and they collapsed in the midst of the desert. They were certain of destruction. While they were in that state, a man appeared before them wearing a robe, with water dripping from his head. They said: 'This man has only recently come from the fertile lands (rif).' He approached them and said: 'O people, what is your condition?' They said: 'You see how our backs have grown weary and our provisions have run out in the midst of this desert, and we do not know how much of it we have crossed or how much remains.' He said: 'What will you give me if I bring you to water that quenches and to green gardens?' They said: 'Your judgment.' He said: 'You must give me your covenants and your pledges that you will not disobey me.' They did so. He led them on and brought them to water that quenches and green gardens. He remained there a little while, then said: 'Come to gardens more lush than these gardens of yours, and to water more refreshing than this water of yours.' Most of the people said: 'We are not able to do this, to the point that we almost cannot.' But a group among them said: 'Did you not make this man your covenant and pledge that you would not disobey him? He has been truthful with you at the beginning of his speech, so the end of his speech is like its beginning.' So they set out with him, and he brought them to green gardens and refreshing water. As for the others, the enemy came upon them during the night, and by morning they were between the slain and the captured."

He also said: "The example of the believer is like the palm tree: it gives good fruit and produces good fruit. And the example of the believer is like a piece of good gold which is put into the fire, blown upon, and comes out good."

Layth narrated from Mujahid, from Ibn Umar, who traced it to the Prophet (ﷺ): "The example of the believer is the example of the palm tree (or 'the bee,' al-nahla): if you consult it, it benefits you; if you walk with it, it benefits you; if you partner with it, it benefits you."

He also said: "The example of the believer and faith is like a horse in its tether: it roams as far as it roams, then returns to its tether. Likewise, the believer may stray as far as he strays, then returns to faith."

He also said: "The example of the believers in their mutual affection and compassion is like the body: when one part of it complains, the rest of it responds with sleeplessness and fever."

He also said: "The example of the hypocrite is like a sheep wandering between two flocks: it charges at this one once and at that one once."

He also said: "The example of the Qur'an is like camels that are tied: if their owner attends to their tethering, he keeps them; if he neglects them, they wander off. When the companion of the Qur'an stands by it, he remembers it; when he does not stand by it, he forgets it."

Musa ibn Ubayda narrated from Ma'iz ibn Suwayd al-Arji, from Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah honor his face), that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The example of the believer who does not complete his prayer is like a woman who became pregnant, and when her time of delivery drew near, she miscarried; so she has neither a pregnancy nor a suckling child. The example of the one who prays is like the merchant: profit does not come to him until his capital comes to him. Likewise, Allah does not accept a voluntary prayer from the one who prays until he performs the obligatory prayer."

Hammad ibn Salama narrated from Ali ibn Zayd, from Aws ibn Khalid, from Abu Hurayra, who traced it to the Prophet (ﷺ): "The example of one who hears wisdom but carries away only its evil is like a man who came to a shepherd and said: 'Hire me a sheep from your flock.' He said: 'Go and take hold of the ear of one of them.' So he went and took hold of the ear of a sheepdog."

Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak said: Abd al-Rahman ibn Yazid ibn Jabir narrated to us, saying: Abu Hurayra told me: "I heard Mu'awiya say from this pulpit: 'I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Nothing remains of this world except trial and tribulation. The example of one's deeds is like a vessel: when its upper part is good, its lower part is good; and when its upper part is bad, its lower part is bad."'"

In the Musnad, from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "A man among those before you was a guest of a people who hosted him. They had a female dog that barked. She said: 'By Allah, I will not bark at my family's guest tonight.' Then her puppies began to howl in her belly. This reached a prophet of theirs, or a ruler among them, and he said: 'The example of this is the example of a community that will come after you, in which its foolish will overpower its wise and its foolish will prevail over its scholars.'"

In Sahih al-Bukhari, from the hadith of al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The example of one who observes the limits of Allah and one who violates them is like a people who drew lots for a ship. Some of them obtained its upper deck and some its lower deck. Those in the lower deck, whenever they needed water, had to pass by those above them. They said: 'If only we bored a hole in our share, we would not harm those above us.' If the others leave them to what they want, they will all perish; and if they take hold of their hands, they will be saved and all will be saved."

In al-Mu'jam al-Kabir, also from him (al-Tabarani), from the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd, he said: "Beware of the small sins, for their example is like a people who camped in the bottom of a valley. One came with a stick, and another with a stick, until they gathered enough to cook their bread. Indeed, small sins, if their doer is seized by them, will destroy him."

In the Musnad, from the hadith of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who traced it to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed, the food of the son of Adam has struck a parable for this world. Look at what comes out of the son of Adam: its dung and its salt. He knows where it ends up."

Abu Muhammad ibn Khallad said: Abdullah ibn Ahmad ibn Ma'dan narrated to us, saying: Yusuf ibn Muslim al-Massisi narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj al-A'war narrated to us, from Abu Bakr al-Hudhali, from al-Hasan, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "I have struck a parable for this world, and for the son of Adam at the time of death. His parable is like a man who had three friends. When death came to him, he said to one of them: 'You were a friend to me, and you were the dearest of the three to me. Now there has descended upon me from the command of Allah what you see. What do you have for me?' He said: 'What do I have? This is the command of Allah, and it has overcome me. I cannot relieve your distress, nor remove your grief, nor delay your hour. But here I am before you; take me as provision that you may carry with you, for it will benefit you.' Then he called the second and said: 'You were a friend to me, and you were the dearest of the three to me. Now there has descended upon me from the command of Allah what you see. What do you have for me?' He said: 'What do I have? This is the command of Allah, and it has overcome me. I cannot relieve your distress, nor remove your grief, nor delay your hour. But I will attend to you in your illness, and when you die I will wash your body thoroughly, renew your shroud, and cover your body and your nakedness.' Then he called the third and said: 'There has descended upon me from the command of Allah what you see. You were the least of the three to me, and I was neglectful toward you, and you were indifferent to me. What do you have?' He said: 'I have my father, your companion and ally in this world and the Hereafter. I will enter your grave with you when you enter it, and I will come out with you when you come out. I will never leave you.'" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "That is his wealth, his family, and his deeds. As for the first, who said 'Take me as provision,' that is his wealth; the second is his family; and the third is his deeds."

It was also narrated with a different wording from the hadith of Ubayy, also: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said one day to his companions: "Do you know the example of one of you, and the example of his wealth, his family, and his deeds?" They said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "The example of one of you, and the example of his family, his wealth, and his deeds, is like a man who had three brothers. When death came to him, he called one of his brothers and said: 'There has descended upon me what you see. What is my due from you, and what do you have for me?' He said: 'For you I will be with you in your illness and will not leave you; I will attend to your affairs. When you die, I will wash you, shroud you, and carry you with those who carry; I will carry you at times and set you down at times. When I return, I will praise you with goodness before those who ask about you here.' This brother is his family. What do you think of him?" They said: "We do not hear anything of value, O Messenger of Allah." Then he said to the other brother: "Do you see what has descended upon me? What is my due from you, and what do you have for me?" He said: "I have no help for you except that you are among the living. When you die, one path will take you and another will take me. This brother is his wealth. How do you see him?" They said: "We do not hear anything of value, O Messenger of Allah." Then he said to his other brother: "Do you see what has descended upon me, and what my family and my wealth could not repel from me? What is my due from you, and what do you have for me?" He said: "I am your companion in your grave, your companion in your loneliness, and I will stand on the Day of Weighing in your scale and make your scale heavy. This brother is his deeds. How do you see him?" They said: "He is the best brother and the best companion, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "The matter is indeed like this."

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) also said: "The example of the good companion is like the example of the bearer of musk: either he will give you some, or you will buy from him, or you will find a pleasant fragrance from him. The example of the bad companion is like the example of the blacksmith's bellows: if its sparks do not reach you, its smoke will reach you."

In the Sahih, from him, he said: "The example of the one who spends and the miser is like two men wearing coats of mail, from their chests to their collarbones. When the spender wants to spend, it expands over him until it covers his fingertips and conceals his footprints. When the miser wants to spend, each ring contracts and clings to its place; he tries to widen it, but it does not widen."

He also said: "The example of those among my community who go out to fight and hasten to receive their rewards is like the mother of Musa (Moses), who nurses her child and receives her wage."

[Section: The Benefit of Striking Parables]

They said: These and similar parables are among those which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) struck to bring the meaning near, to make it understood, to convey it to the mind of the listener, and to bring it before the soul in the form of the parable through which it was struck. For it may be closer to his understanding, comprehension, retention, and recall, by recalling its counterpart. The soul is perfectly at ease with counterparts and likenesses, and it recoils from strangeness, isolation, and the lack of a counterpart. Thus, in parables there is a comforting of the soul, quick acceptance, and submission to the truth for which a parable has been struck, a matter that no one denies or rejects. Whenever parables appear to the soul, the meaning becomes more manifest and clear. Parables are witnesses to the intended meaning and attest to it. They are like ﴿a seed that sends out its shoot, then strengthens it, so it grows thick and stands firm on its stalk﴾ [al-Fath 48:29], and they are the distinguishing feature of reason, its essence, and its fruit.

[The Difference Between the Parables Struck by Allah and His Messenger and Qiyas (Analogical Reasoning)]

But where in the parables that Allah and His Messenger struck in this manner do we find the basis for holding that the bridal gift (sadaq) may not be less than three dirhams or ten, by analogy and comparison with the minimum value for which a thief's hand is cut off? This resembles riddles and puzzles more than parables struck for understanding. As the imam of hadith, Muhammad ibn Isma'il al-Bukhari, said in his al-Jami' al-Sahih: "Chapter: On one who likens a known principle to a clearly established principle, when Allah has explained the ruling for both, so that the listener may understand." We do not deny these parables struck by Allah and His Messenger, nor do we fail to recognize what they intend. Rather, we deny that the obligation of a blood payment (dam) for one who removes three or four hairs from his body or head may be derived from the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And do not shave your heads until the offering reaches its place. But whoever among you is ill or has an ailment of the head should pay a ransom of fasting, charity, or sacrifice﴾ [al-Baqara 2:196], and that the verse indicates this. Nor do we accept that the Prophet's (ﷺ) words on the Zakat al-Fitr (the obligatory charity at the end of Ramadan): "A sa' of dates, or a sa' of barley, or a sa' of dried curds, or a sa' of wheat, or a sa' of raisins," imply that if one gave a sa' of myrobalan it would be permissible, and that it indicates this by way of analogy and reasoning. Nor do we accept that his (ﷺ) words: "The child belongs to the bed (firash)," can be understood from its implication to mean that if a guardian said in the presence of a judge: "I have married you to my daughter" (while he is in the farthest east and she is in the farthest west), and the man said: "I accept this marriage, and she is divorced three times," and then she bore a child more than six months later, that child is his son, because she became his bed (firash) merely by his saying "I accept this marriage." Yet if he had a concubine whom he had intercourse with night and day, she would not be his bed; and if she bore a child, that child would not be attributed to him unless he claimed it and acknowledged it. If he did not acknowledge it, then it is not his child.

**Translation of Ibn al-Qayyim's Commentary on Surah 4, Verse 59 (Part 5 of 7)**

And where is it understood from his ﷺ saying: "Indeed, in the killing by mistake that resembles deliberate killing (shibh al-'amd), what was done with a whip or a stick is one hundred camels," that if he struck him with a catapult stone (hajar al-manjaniq), or with a blacksmith's hammer, or with large iron maces, until his brain was mixed with his flesh and bone, this would be a mistaken killing resembling deliberate killing, which does not necessitate retaliation (qawad)?

And where is it understood from his ﷺ saying: "Avert the prescribed punishments (hudud) from the Muslims as much as you can. If there is a way out for him, then let him go, for the imam's erring in pardon is better for him than his erring in punishment," that whoever marries his mother, his daughter, or his sister and has intercourse with her, there is no hadd punishment upon him? And that this is understood from his saying: "Avert the hudud by doubts (shubuhat)." So this has the meaning of the doubt by which the hudud are averted, which is doubt in the object (al-mahall), or in the agent (al-fa'il), or in belief (al-i'tiqad). And if this were presented to the understanding of any person of all the worlds, he would not understand it from this wording in any way whatsoever.

And that whoever has intercourse with his maternal aunt or paternal aunt by right of ownership (milk al-yamin) has no hadd punishment upon him, even though he knows that she is his aunt and that God has forbidden it. This is understood from "avert the hudud by doubts." And many times this, which cannot nearly be enumerated, [is also understood in this way].

So this illustration and comparison is what we reject, and we reject that there could be in the words of God and His Messenger any indication of such understanding in any way.

They said: From where is it understood from the saying of the Exalted: "Indeed, in the livestock there is a lesson for you" (Surah an-Nahl 16:66), and from His saying: "So take heed, O people of insight" (Surah al-Hashr 59:2), the prohibition of selling kishk with milk, or selling vinegar with grapes, and the like?

They said: And the Exalted has said: "Whatever you differ about, its judgment is with God" (Surah ash-Shura 42:10). He did not say "with your analogies and your opinions." God has never made the opinions and analogies of men a judge among the community, ever.

They said: And the Exalted has said: "It is not for a believing man or a believing woman, when God and His Messenger have decreed a matter, that they should have any choice in their affair" (Surah al-Ahzab 33:36). He only prohibited them from choice in the face of His judgment and the judgment of His Messenger, not in the face of the opinions of men, their analogies, and their conjectures. The Exalted has commanded His Messenger to follow only what is revealed to him, saying: "I follow only what is revealed to me" (Surah al-An'am 6:50), and He said: "And judge between them by what God has revealed" (Surah al-Ma'idah 5:49). The Exalted also said: "Or do they have partners who have prescribed for them in religion what God has not permitted?" (Surah ash-Shura 42:21). They said: This text indicates that whatever God has not permitted in religion is the legislation of another, which is false.

They said: The Prophet ﷺ has reported from his Lord, blessed and exalted is He, that everything He is silent about regarding obligation or prohibition is a pardon (afw) which He has pardoned for His servants. It is permitted by the permissibility of pardon. Therefore it is not lawful to prohibit it or to make it obligatory by analogy with what He has made obligatory or prohibited, on the basis of a common factor between them. For that would necessitate the complete abolition of this category and its cancellation. For what is silent about must necessarily have some resemblance to the prohibited, or a common attribute with it, or some resemblance to the obligatory. So if it were permitted to attach it to them, there would be no category that has been pardoned, and what He was silent about would not have been pardoned. Rather, what He was silent about would have been prohibited by analogy with what He prohibited. This cannot be avoided. In that case, prohibiting what He was silent about would be a change of His ruling. The Exalted has condemned whoever changes what he was commanded to say. So whoever changes a ruling other than the one prescribed for him is even more deserving of condemnation. The Prophet ﷺ has said: "Indeed, among the greatest of crimes committed by the Muslims against the Muslims is for one who asks about something that was not prohibited, and then it is prohibited for the people because of his asking." If this applies to one who explicitly caused the Lawgiver's prohibition by his question about the ruling on what was left unmentioned, then how much more so for one who prohibits what was left unmentioned by his own analogy and opinion?

It clarifies this: that what is left unmentioned, since it is a pardon which God has pardoned for His servants, and since searching for it would be a cause for God's prohibiting it because of what it entails of a prohibition, not merely because of asking about its ruling. God had pardoned this and been lenient with His servants in it, just as He pardons what contains corruption in their deeds and words. It is known that His silence about mentioning a general term which prohibits something indicates that it is a pardon. So whoever prohibits it by asking about the reason for the prohibition and by analogizing it to what is prohibited by explicit text is more deserving of condemnation than one who asked about its ruling out of need for it, so that it was prohibited because of his asking. Rather, the obligation upon him was not to search for it or ask about its ruling, relying on God's silence about His pardon of it. In the same way, the obligation upon him is not to prohibit what is left unmentioned without the text, the text by which God prohibited its root, which it is attached to.

They said: The Book of God has also indicated this, where He says: "O you who believe, do not ask about things which, if they were disclosed to you, would distress you. And if you ask about them while the Qur'an is being revealed, they will be disclosed to you. God has pardoned them, and God is Forgiving and Forbearing" (Surah al-Ma'idah 5:101). "A people before you asked about them, then they became disbelievers because of them" (Surah al-Ma'idah 5:102). The Prophet ﷺ has also said in the sound hadith: "Leave me as I have left you, for those before you were destroyed because of the abundance of their questions and their disagreement with their prophets. So when I forbid you from something, avoid it, and when I command you to do something, do of it as much as you are able." So he commanded them to leave off asking as long as he left them alone. There is no difference in this between his life and after his death. So we are commanded to leave him ﷺ and what he has stated explicitly. Thus we should not say to him: "Why did you prohibit such-and-such?" in order to attach to it what he was silent about. Rather, this is a greater disobedience than asking him about the ruling on something he did not rule on. Consider it carefully, for it is clear.

It is also indicated by his saying in the same hadith: "When I forbid you from something, avoid it, and when I command you with a command, do of it as much as you are able." So he made matters three, with no fourth: something commanded, for which the obligation upon them is to do it according to their ability; something forbidden, for which the obligation upon them is to avoid it entirely; and something left unmentioned, which should not be subjected to questioning or investigation. This ruling is not specific to his lifetime alone, nor does it apply only to the Companions to the exclusion of those who came after them. Rather, it is obligatory upon us as well to carry out his command according to our ability, to avoid his prohibition, and to leave off searching and investigating what he was silent about. Leaving this off is not ignorance of or disparagement of his ruling, but an affirmation of the ruling of pardon, which is general permissibility and the removal of hardship from the one who does it. The hadith has encompassed all categories of religion, for they are either obligatory, or prohibited, or permitted. The disliked (makruh) and the recommended (mustahabb) are branches of these three, not outside permissibility. And the Exalted has said: "So when We have recited it, follow its recitation" (Surah al-Qiyamah 75:18), "Then upon Us is its explanation" (Surah al-Qiyamah 75:19). So He entrusted its explanation to Himself, the Exalted, not to the analogizers and the advocates of opinion. And the Exalted has said: "Say: Have you considered what God has sent down to you of provision, and you made of it lawful and unlawful? Say: Did God permit you, or do you invent falsehood against God?" (Surah Yunus 10:59). So He divided the ruling into two parts: a part He permitted, which is the truth, and a part falsely attributed to Him, which is what He did not permit. So where did He permit us to analogize the oak (ballut) to dates regarding the operation of ribā in it? Or to analogize tin (qasdir) to gold and silver, or mustard to wheat? If God and His Messenger have instructed us in this, then it is hearing and obeying God and His Messenger. Otherwise, we say to our opponents: "Or were you witnesses when God enjoined this upon you?" (Surah al-An'am 6:144). So whatever has not come to us as an instruction from God through the tongue of His Messenger ﷺ is pure falsehood. God has commanded us to refer whatever we dispute to Him and to His Messenger ﷺ. He has never permitted us to refer that to opinion, analogy, following an imam's taqlid, dreams, unveilings, inspirations, a whisper of the heart, juristic preference (istihsan), rational reasoning, the law of the diwan, the politics of kings, or the customs of the people, which are no more harmful to the laws of the Muslims than these. All of these are false idols (taghut). Whoever takes them as a judge, or calls his opponent to judgment by them, has judged by the taghut.

The Exalted has said: "So do not strike forth similitudes for God. Indeed, God knows, and you do not know" (Surah an-Nahl 16:74). They said: Whoever reflects on this verse with true reflection will see that it is an explicit text nullifying and prohibiting analogy. For analogy in its entirety is the striking of similitudes for religion, and the illustration of what has no text by what has a text. Whoever illustrates what God has not stated as prohibited or obligatory by what He has prohibited or made obligatory has struck similitudes for God. Had the Exalted known that what He was silent about was like what He stated explicitly, He would have informed us of it, and He would not have neglected it: "And your Lord was never forgetful" (Surah Maryam 19:64). And He would make clear to us what we should guard against, as He informed about Himself when He says, the Exalted: "And God would not send astray a people after He has guided them until He makes clear to them what they should avoid" (Surah at-Tawbah 9:115). But He has left it to our opinions and our analogies, some of which contradict others. This one analogizes what he holds to what he claims is its counterpart, and then his opponent comes and analogizes the opposite of his analogy in every respect, and shows a common attribute like the one his opponents showed, or more apparent than it. It is impossible that two conflicting analogies both come from God, and neither is more preferable than the other. Therefore neither of them is from Him. This alone is sufficient to nullify analogy.

The Exalted has also said: "We did not send any messenger except in the language of his people, to make things clear to them" (Surah Ibrahim 14:4), and He said: "That you may explain to the people what has been sent down to them" (Surah an-Nahl 16:44). So everything the Messenger of God ﷺ explained was from his Lord, the Exalted. He explained it by His command and permission. We know with certainty that every name in the language refers to what it names in that language: the name "wheat" does not encompass mustard, the name "dates" does not encompass oak, the names "gold" and "silver" do not encompass tin. The determination of the minimum value for the theft (nisab al-sariqah) does not include the determination of the bridal gift (mahr). The prohibition of eating carrion does not indicate that a good believer, in God's sight, living or dead, becomes impure and wicked when he dies. And this [analogy] is, away from the explanation which God entrusted to His Messenger and sent him with, the furthest thing and the most contrary to it. So it is definitely not something the Messenger was sent with, and therefore it is not from the religion.

The Prophet ﷺ has said: "God has not sent any prophet except that it was incumbent upon him to direct his community to the best of what he knows for them, and to warn them against the worst of what he knows for them." Had analogy and opinion been good for them, he would have directed them to it and guided them to it, and he would have said to them: "If I obligate something upon you or prohibit it, then analogize from it whatever has between it and it a common attribute or something similar, or what indicates this or entails it." And he would have warned them against that with the utmost warning, as you will see, God willing. The language has firmly established each name for what it names, and not for anything else. God, the Exalted, sent Muhammad ﷺ only in Arabic, the language which the Arabs understand from its own tongue. So when God, the Exalted, in His Book, or His Messenger, explicitly names one of the names and attaches to it a ruling among the rulings, it is necessary that this ruling not apply except to what that name requires. And nothing that the name requires may be excluded from that ruling. Whatever goes beyond that is an addition to the religion, and whatever falls short of it is a deficiency in the religion. The first is analogy, and the second is false specification (takhsis). Both are not from the religion. Whoever does not hold to the texts will at times add to the text what is not part of it and say: "This is analogy." And at other times he will omit some of what it requires and exclude it from its ruling and say: "This is specification." And at other times he will abandon the text entirely and say: "Action is not upon it," or say: "This is contrary to analogy," or "contrary to the principles."

They said: If analogy were part of the religion, its adherents would be the most conforming to the hadiths, and the more deeply a man went into it, the more he would be strict in following the hadiths and reports.

They say: "We observe that the more deeply a man immerses himself in analogy, the more his opposition to the Sunan (the established prophetic practices) intensifies. We see opposition to the Sunan and the reports only among the people of opinion (ra'y) and analogy (qiyas). How many sound and explicit Sunnah have been nullified by them! And how many reports have had their rulings effaced because of them!"

So the Sunan and the reports, in the eyes of the proponents of opinion and analogy, are empty upon their foundations, their rulings suspended, cut off from their authority and governance. They retain the name, while the ruling belongs to others. From them comes the coinage and the sermon, while command and prohibition belong to others. Otherwise, why was the hadith on 'araya (the permission of selling dates on the tree for dried dates) abandoned? And the hadith on the division of time among wives at the beginning of marriage, that a wife is entitled to seven nights if she is a virgin and three if she is a previously married woman, after which he divides equally? And the hadith on the banishment of an unmarried fornicator?

And the hadith on making a stipulation in Hajj and the permissibility of exiting the state of ihram by stipulation? And the hadith on wiping over the two socks? And the hadith of 'Imran ibn Husayn and Abu Hurayrah that the speech of one who forgets or is ignorant does not invalidate the prayer? And the hadith on returning a found article (luqatah) to the one who comes and describes its container, its tie, and its wrapping? And the hadith of the musarrah (the animal whose udder is artificially swollen)? And the hadith of casting lots among slaves when they are freed during illness and the third (of the estate) cannot cover them? And the hadith of the option of the session (khiyar al-majlis) in sales? And the hadith that one who eats forgetfully should complete the fast? And the hadith that one who catches the sunrise after having prayed one rak'ah of Subh should complete the prayer? And the hadith on fasting on behalf of the deceased? And the hadith on performing Hajj on behalf of a sick person who has no hope of recovery? And the hadith on judging by the qafah (judgment by tracking and physiognomy)?

And the hadith of one who finds his property with a man who has become bankrupt? And the hadith prohibiting the sale of fresh dates for dried dates? And the hadith on selling the mudabbar (a slave freed upon his master's death)? And the hadith of judging by one witness together with an oath? And the hadith that the child belongs to the bed (of the husband) when born of a female slave, which was the cause of the hadith? And the hadith giving a boy the choice between his parents when they separate? And the hadith on cutting off the hand of a thief for a quarter dinar? And the hadith on stoning the two People of the Book for adultery? And the hadith that one who marries his father's wife is to be ordered to have his neck struck and his property taken? And the hadith "A believer is not killed for an unbeliever"? And the hadith "Allah curses the one who performs tahlil (marrying a divorced woman to make her lawful again) and the one for whom it is performed"? And the hadith "There is no marriage except with a guardian (wali)"?

And the hadith of the woman divorced three times, that she has no right to lodging or maintenance? And the hadith "He freed Safiyyah and made her freedom her dowry," and the hadith "Give her a dowry, even if it is an iron ring"? And the hadith permitting the eating of horse meat? And the hadith "Every intoxicant is forbidden"? And the hadith "There is no charity (zakat) on less than five wasq"? And the hadith on muzara'ah (sharecropping) and musaqah (irrigation partnership)? And the hadith "The slaughter of the fetus is the slaughter of its mother"? And the hadith "The pledge may be ridden and milked"? And the hadith prohibiting making vinegar from wine? And the hadith on dividing the spoils: a foot soldier receives one share and a horseman three? And the hadith "A single suck or two sucks do not establish prohibition by milk-kinship"? And the hadiths on the sanctity of Madinah? And the hadith on marking the sacrificial animal (ish'ar)? And the hadith "If the muhrim cannot find an izar, let him wear trousers"? And the hadith prohibiting a man from preferring some of his children over others, that it is injustice and that testimony regarding it is not permitted? And the hadith "You and your wealth belong to your father"? And the hadith of the qasamah (oath of fifty men in cases of unknown killing)? And the hadith on ablution from eating camel meat? And the hadiths on wiping over the turban.

And the hadith ordering the repetition of the prayer for one who prays alone behind the row? And the hadith "One who enters while the imam is delivering the khutbah should pray the tahiyyat al-masjid (greeting of the mosque)"? And the hadith on the funeral prayer in absentia? And the hadith on saying "Amin" aloud in prayer? And the hadith permitting a father to take back what he gave his child, while no one else may take back a gift? And the hadith that a black dog cuts off the prayer? And the hadith on going out to the 'Id the next day if one learns of the 'Id after midday? And the hadith on sprinkling urine of a boy who has not yet eaten food? And the hadith on praying over a grave? And the hadith that one who plants in people's land without their permission has no share of the crop, but is owed his expenses?

And the hadith of Jabir's sale of his camel with the stipulation of its riding? And the hadith prohibiting the skins of predators? And the hadith "None of you should prevent his neighbor from driving a wooden beam into his wall"? And the hadith that the most deserving of conditions to be fulfilled are those by which intimacy is made lawful? And the hadith that one who sells a slave who has property, his property belongs to the seller? And the hadith that if a man embraces Islam while having two sisters as wives, he chooses whichever he wishes? And the hadith on performing witr while riding? And the hadith that every animal with fangs among the predators is forbidden? And the hadith that it is from the Sunnah to place the right hand over the left in prayer? And the hadith "A prayer is not valid in which a man does not straighten his spine in bowing and prostration"? And the hadiths on raising the hands in prayer at bowing and rising from it? And the hadiths on the opening supplication (istiftah).

And the hadith "The Prophet (ﷺ) had two pauses in prayer," and the hadith that its opening is takbir and its conclusion is taslim? And the hadith on carrying a child in prayer? And the hadiths on casting lots? And the hadiths on 'aqiqah? And the hadith "If a man looks into your house without your permission..."? And the hadith "Would he place his hand in your mouth to bite it as a stallion bites?" And the hadith "Bilal calls the adhan at night"? And the hadith prohibiting fasting on Friday? And the hadith prohibiting slaughter with a tooth or a nail? And the hadiths on the eclipse prayer and the prayer for rain? And the hadith prohibiting the stud fee for a stallion? And the hadith that a muhrim who dies should not have his head covered nor be perfumed? — and up to many times this number of hadiths whose abandonment was for the sake of saying analogy and opinion?

So if analogy were true, its people would have been the most faithful of the Ummah to the hadiths, and no one would have been known to abandon a single hadith except because of an abrogating text. Hence, whenever we see that the more deeply someone immerses himself in analogy and opinion, the more he opposes the sound and explicit hadiths, we know that analogy is not part of the religion, and that something for whose sake the Sunan are abandoned is most manifestly contrary to the religion. If analogy were from Allah, it would conform to the Sunnah in the greatest conformity, and its proponents would not oppose a single hadith from it; they would have been happier with it than the people of hadith. Let them show the people of hadith and reports one sound hadith that they have opposed, as we have shown them just now the Sunnah they opposed because of analogy.

They say: Allah took the covenant from the People of the Book and after them from us, that we should not say about Allah except the truth. If these conflicting and contradictory analogies, which refute one another such that the examiner cannot tell which of them is truly correct, were true, they would be consistent, confirming one another, like the Sunnah whose parts confirm one another. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And Allah establishes the truth by His words﴾ [Yunus: 82], not by our opinions or our analogies. And He said: ﴿And Allah speaks the truth, and He guides to the way﴾ [al-Ahzab: 4]. So whatever He has not said, nor guided to, is not from the truth. And He the Exalted said: ﴿But if they do not respond to you, know that they only follow their desires﴾ [al-Qasas: 50]. Thus He divided matters into two categories with no third: following what the Messenger called to, or following desire.

[Section: The Prophet did not command analogy but forbade it]

The Messenger (ﷺ) never called his Ummah to analogy at all. Rather, it is authentically reported from him that he rebuked 'Umar and Usamah for pure analogy regarding the two garments he sent to them. Usamah wore his garment, analogizing wearing it to ownership, benefiting from it, selling it, and clothing others with it. 'Umar returned his, analogizing owning it to wearing it. So Usamah permitted by analogy, and 'Umar prohibited by analogy. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) invalidated each of the two analogies. He said to 'Umar: "I only sent it to you so that you might benefit from it," and he said to Usamah: "I did not send it to you so that you would wear it, but I sent it to you so that you would cut it into head-coverings for your women." The Prophet (ﷺ) had only given a precise command concerning silk, prohibiting its wearing alone. So they analogized, and erred in their analogies: one analogized wearing to owning, and 'Umar analogized owning to wearing. The Prophet (ﷺ) made clear that what he prohibited of wearing does not extend to anything else, and what he permitted of owning does not extend to wearing. This is precisely the invalidation of analogy.

And authentically reported from him is what Abu Tha'labah al-Khushani narrated, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah has prescribed obligations, so do not neglect them; He has set limits, so do not transgress them; He has forbidden things, so do not violate them; and He has remained silent about things out of mercy for you, not out of forgetfulness, so do not search for them." This address, as its beginning is general to the Companions and those after them, so is its end. It is not permitted for us to investigate what he remained silent about, in order to make it forbidden or obligatory.

'Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak said: Isa ibn Yunus narrated to us from Jarir ibn 'Uthman from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Jubayr ibn Nufayr from his father from 'Awf ibn Malik al-Ashja'i, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "My Ummah will split into seventy-some sects, the greatest of them in trial against my Ummah being a people who analogize matters by their opinion, so they make lawful what is unlawful and make unlawful what is lawful." Qasim ibn Asbagh said: Muhammad ibn Isma'il al-Tirmidhi narrated to us, Nu'aym ibn Hammad narrated to us, 'Abd Allah narrated to us, and he mentioned it. All of these are imams, trustworthy, and memorizers, except Jarir ibn 'Uthman, who was inclined away from 'Ali. Nevertheless al-Bukhari relied on him in his Sahih, and it is reported from him that he disavowed what was attributed to him of deviation from 'Ali. Nu'aym ibn Hammad is a great imam, and he was a sword against the Jahmiyyah, and al-Bukhari narrated from him in his Sahih.

It is also authentically reported from him, with a authenticity approaching mass transmission, that he said: "Leave me with what I have left you. Those before you were destroyed only by the abundance of their questions and their disputing with their prophets. What I forbid you, avoid; and what I command you, do of it what you are able." This hadith includes that what he commanded with a command of obligation is obligatory, and what he forbade is prohibited, and what he remained silent about is pardoned and permitted. Thus everything other than that is invalid. Analogy falls outside these three categories, so it is invalid. The analogized matter is undoubtedly one he remained silent about, so it is undoubtedly pardoned. Therefore attaching it to the prohibited is making unlawful what Allah has pardoned.

In his saying "Leave me with what I have left you" is clear evidence that what has no text is neither forbidden nor obligatory. The hadith also shows that his commands are for obligation until something comes that removes this, or clarifies that he intended recommendation; and that what we cannot do falls away from us.

Ibn al-Mughallis narrated to us: 'Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, Abu Qilabah al-Raqashi narrated to us, Abu al-Rabi' al-Zahrani narrated to us, Sayf ibn Harun al-Burjumi narrated to us from Sulayman al-Taymi from Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi from Salman (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about things, and he said: 'The lawful is what Allah has made lawful, the unlawful is what Allah has made unlawful, and what He has remained silent about is among what He has pardoned.'" This is a good isnad, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ). And Allah is the One sought for help, and upon Him is reliance.

[Section: On the virtue of the imams]

The second matter: knowing the virtue of the imams of Islam, their stations, their rights, and their ranks, and that their merit, knowledge, and sincerity toward Allah and His Messenger does not oblige accepting everything they said. What occurred in their fatwas, in matters where what the Messenger brought was hidden from them, so they spoke according to the extent of their knowledge while the truth lay in the opposite, does not oblige discarding their sayings entirely, belittling them, or attacking them. These are two extremes that deviate from the right path, and the straight course lies between them. We do not declare them sinners nor infallible. We do not follow them in the manner of the Rafidah regarding 'Ali, nor in the manner of those who revile the two Shaykhs (Abu Bakr and 'Umar). Rather, we follow their own way regarding those before them among the Companions: they neither declare them sinners nor treat them as infallible, and they neither accept all their sayings nor discard them.

How can they object to us over the four Imams following a path that they themselves follow with regard to the four Caliphs and the rest of the Companions? These two matters do not conflict for one whom Allah has opened his heart to Islam. They conflict only for one of two men: one who is ignorant of the rank and virtue of the Imams, or one who is ignorant of the reality of the Shari'ah with which Allah sent His Messenger. Whoever has knowledge of the Shari'ah and of reality knows with certainty that a man of great standing, who has a righteous past and good deeds in Islam and a high place in Islam and among its people, may nonetheless commit a slip or a lapse. In that matter he is excused, and indeed rewarded for his ijtihad (independent reasoning). Therefore it is not permissible to follow him in that error, nor is it permissible for his standing, his leadership and his rank to be discarded from the hearts of the Muslims.

Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak said: "I was in Kufa, and they debated with me about nabidh (a date-based drink) on which the scholars differ. I said to them: 'Come, let whoever among you wishes to argue for the permission cite any Companion of the Prophet (ﷺ) he chooses. If the one who refutes him cannot show a sound chain of narration from that man, then argue.' They produced for every permission a Companion, and we brought them a chain for it. When none of them had anything left except Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, their argument from him concerning the strong (intoxicating) nabidh was not supported by anything authentically transmitted from him. What is authentically transmitted from him is only that he did not prepare nabidh in the green jar."

Ibn al-Mubarak said: "I then said to the one who argued from him for the permission: 'You fool! Return to what we have described. If Ibn Mas'ud were sitting here and said, "It is lawful for you," and what we have described from the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions concerning the strong drink were before you, you should still have been cautious and fearful.' Someone said: 'O Abu Abd al-Rahman, what of al-Nakha'i and al-Sha'bi, and he named several others besides them? Did they drink what is forbidden?' I said to them: 'Leave aside naming men during a debate. Many a man in Islam has such-and-such virtues, and there may be a slip from him. Would it be permissible for anyone to argue by it?' If you refuse, then what is your view of 'Ata', Tawus, Jabir ibn Zayd, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ikrimah?' They said: 'They were the best (of people).' I said: 'What is your view on exchanging a dirham for two dirhams, hand to hand?' They said: 'It is forbidden.' I said: 'These men regarded it as lawful. Did they die while consuming what is forbidden?' Then they were bewildered and their argument was cut off."

Ibn al-Mubarak said: "Al-Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman informed me, saying: 'My father saw me reciting poetry and said: "My son, do not recite poetry." I said: "Father, al-Hasan (al-Basri) used to recite poetry, and Ibn Sirin used to recite it." He said: "My son, if you take the worst of what is in al-Hasan and the worst of what is in Ibn Sirin, all the evil will be gathered in you."'"

Shaykh al-Islam (Ibn Taymiyya) said: "What Ibn al-Mubarak mentioned is agreed upon among the scholars. There is no one among the eminent Imams, from the earliest foremost generations and those after them, except that he has sayings and actions in which the Sunnah was hidden from him."

I say: Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr said at the beginning of his Istidhkar.

Shaykh al-Islam said: "This is a vast domain that cannot be counted. Yet this does not diminish their standing, nor does it make it permissible to follow them in those matters." Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And if you disagree concerning anything, refer it back to Allah and the Messenger﴾ [An-Nisa: 59]. Mujahid, al-Hakam ibn Utaybah, Malik and others said: "No one among the creation of Allah is there except that his statements may be taken or left, except the Prophet (ﷺ)." Sulayman al-Taymi said: "If you take the permission of every scholar, all evil will be gathered in you." Ibn Abd al-Barr said: "This is a consensus, and I know of no disagreement concerning it. And there have been reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions, on this meaning, things that deserve reflection."

Kathir ibn Abdullah ibn Amr ibn Awf al-Muzani narrated from his father, from his grandfather, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Indeed I fear for my Ummah after me three deeds.' They said: 'And what are they, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'I fear for them the slip of the scholar, the judgment of the oppressive ruler, and a followed desire.'"

Ziyad ibn Hudayr said: Umar said: "Three things demolish the religion: the slip of a scholar, the argument of a hypocrite with the Qur'an, and misguiding leaders."

al-Hasan said: Abu al-Darda' said: "Among what I fear for you is the slip of the scholar and the argument of the hypocrite with the Qur'an, though the Qur'an is true, and upon the Qur'an there are signposts like the markers of the road."

Mu'adh ibn Jabal used to say in his sermon every day, and he rarely failed to say it: "Allah is the just Judge. The doubters are destroyed. Indeed, behind you are trials in which wealth will abound and the Qur'an will be opened up, until the believer, the hypocrite, the woman, the child, the black and the red will all read it. Soon one of them will say: 'I have read the Qur'an, and I do not think people will follow me until I innovate something other than it for them.' So beware of what is innovated, for every innovation is misguidance. Beware of the deviation of the wise man, for Satan may speak through the tongue of the wise man with a word of misguidance, and the hypocrite may speak a word of truth. So receive the truth from whoever brings it, for upon the truth there is a light." They said: "What is the deviation of the wise man?" He said: "It is a word that alarms you and that you deny, and you say, 'What is this?' So beware of his deviation, and do not let it turn you away from him, for he will soon return and go back to the truth. Knowledge and faith have their place until the Day of Resurrection, and whoever seeks them will find them."

Salman al-Farisi said: "How will you be concerning three things: the slip of a scholar, the argument of a hypocrite with the Qur'an, and a worldly matter that will cut your necks?" As for the slip of the scholar: if he is guided, do not follow him in your religion, saying 'we will do as so-and-so does'; and if he errs, do not despair of him, lest you help Satan against him. As for the argument of the hypocrite with the Qur'an: the Qur'an has signposts like the signposts of the road; what you recognize from it, take; and what you do not know, entrust it to Allah the Exalted. As for a worldly matter that will cut your necks: look at those below you, and do not look at those above you."

It is reported from Ibn Abbas: "Woe to the followers because of the stumbles of the scholar." It was said: "How is that?" He said: "The scholar says something by his own opinion, then he finds someone who knows more about the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) than he does, so he abandons his statement, but the followers continue on it." Abu Umar narrated all these reports and others.

If we have been warned of the slip of the scholar, and it has been said to us that it is among the things we most fear for ourselves, and we are commanded in addition not to turn away from the truth because of it, then it is obligatory upon whoever Allah has opened his heart to Islam, when a weak statement from some of the Imams reaches him, that he should not relate it to one who will adopt it. Rather, he should remain silent about mentioning it if he is certain of its authenticity; otherwise he should withhold acceptance of it. For many things are attributed to the Imams that have no reality. And many rulings are derived by some followers from the principle of their leader, although if that Imam had seen that they lead to such a thing, he would not have committed to it. Moreover, the necessary implication of a school is not itself the school's doctrine, although the necessary implication of a text is true, because the Lawgiver cannot be subject to contradiction; so the necessary implication of his word is true. As for others, it is not impossible for one of them to say a thing while its necessary implication remains hidden from him, and had he known that this was its necessary implication, he would not have said it. Therefore it is not permissible to say: "This is his school," when he has not said it. And everyone who has knowledge of the Shari'ah and its worth, and of the virtue of the Imams and their standing, their knowledge, their piety and their sincere counsel to the religion, is certain that if they had witnessed this matter of ruses (hiyal) and the manipulation of the religion to which it leads, they would have decisively declared them forbidden.
