What further clarifies this is that those scholars who issued fatwas on some matters of ruses and derived that from some of their principles would, if the reports from the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions concerning this had reached them, certainly have retracted that, for they were at the utmost in fairness, and each of them would return from his opinion even without that. Many of them have stated this explicitly, even though they were all unanimous upon it.

al-Shafi'i said: "When a hadith is authentically reported from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), throw my opinion against the wall." And although this is al-Shafi'i's expression, it is the expression of the whole community. Among the principles upon which the Imams agreed is that the widely spread sayings of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) are not abandoned except by something of equal weight. This clarifies that the prohibition of ruses is a definitive matter and not one of the paths of ijtihad; for had it been a path of ijtihad, the Companions, the Successors and the Imams would not have spoken to the practitioners of ruses with that harsh speech of which we have mentioned a small part out of much. The salaf agreed that they are a newly invented innovation (bid'ah). Therefore it is not permissible to follow one who issues fatwas based on them, it is obligatory to annul his ruling, and it is not permissible to direct the layman to one who issues fatwas with them. Imam Ahmad explicitly stated all of this, and there is no disagreement among the Imams about it. Just as it is not permissible to follow the Meccans and the Kufans on the matters of mut'ah (temporary marriage), sarf (currency exchange) and nabidh, and it is not permissible to follow some of the Medinans on the matter of the latrines and of having intercourse with women in their posteriors. Rather, according to the jurists of hadith, whoever drinks the disputed nabidh is subject to the hadd (prescribed punishment), and this is beyond denouncing with the tongue. Indeed, according to the jurists of Medina he is deemed a fasiq (grossly sinful), and his testimony is not accepted. This refutes the statement of one who said: "There is no denunciation in disputed matters," and this contradicts the consensus of the Imams; no Imam of the Muslim Imams is known to have said that. Imam Ahmad explicitly stated that whoever marries his daughter from fornication is to be killed. Al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Malik do not hold the view of Abu Hanifa regarding one who marries his mother and his daughter, that the prescribed punishment is averted from him due to the doubt that averts the hadd. Rather, according to Imam Ahmad (may Allah be pleased with him) he is to be killed, while according to al-Shafi'i and Malik he is to receive the hadd for fornication in this case. Yet those who permit mut'ah and sarf have a Sunnah on their side, even though it has been abrogated, whereas the practitioners of ruses have no Sunnah on their side, no report from a Companion, and no sound analogy.

فَأقْسَمَ: أنَّهم لا يُؤْمِنُونَ حَتّى يُحَكِّمُوا رَسُولَهُ، وحَتّى يَرْتَفِعَ الحَرَجُ مِن نُفُوسِهِمْ مِن حُكْمِهِ، وحَتّى يُسَلِّمُوا لِحُكْمِهِ تَسْلِيمًا. وهَذا حَقِيقَةُ الرِّضا بِحُكْمِهِ.

فالتَّحْكِيمُ: في مَقامِ الإسْلامِ (Islam). وانْتِفاءُ الحَرَجِ: في مَقامِ الإيمانِ (Iman). والتَّسْلِيمُ: في مَقامِ الإحْسانِ (Ihsan).

وَمَتّى خالَطَ القَلْبَ بَشاشَةُ الإيمانِ، واكْتَحَلَتْ بَصِيرَتُهُ بِحَقِيقَةِ اليَقِينِ، وحَيّى بِرُوحِ الوَحْيِ، وتَمَهَّدَتْ طَبِيعَتُهُ، وانْقَلَبَتِ النَّفْسُ الأمّارَةُ مُطَمَئِنَّةً راضِيَةً وادِعَةً، وتَلَقّى أحْكامَ الرَّبِّ تَعالى بِصَدْرٍ واسِعٍ مُنْشَرِحٍ مُسْلِمٍ: فَقَدْ رَضِيَ كُلَّ الرِّضا بِهَذا القَضاءِ الدِّينِيِّ المَحْبُوبِ لِلَّهِ ولِرَسُولِهِ.

(فائدة)

أقسم سبحانه بنفسه المقدسة قسمًا مؤكدًا بالنفي قبله على عدم إيمان الخلق حتى يحكموا رسوله في كل ما شجر بينهم من الأصول والفروع وأحكام الشرع وأحكام المعاد وسائر الصفات وغيرها، ولم يثبت لهم الإيمان بمجرد هذا التحكيم حتى ينتفي عنهم الحرج، وهو ضيق الصدر، وتنشرح صدورهم لحكمه كل الانشراح، وتنفسح له كل الانفساح، وتقبله كل القبول، ولم يثبت لهم الإيمان.

بذلك أيضًا حتى ينضاف إليه مقابلة حكمه بالرضى والتسليم، وعدم المنازعة، وانتفاء المعارضة والاعتراض. فهنا قد يحكم الرجل غيره وعنده حرج من حكمه، ولا يلزم من انتفاء الحرج والرضا والتسليم والانقياد، إذ قد يحكمه وينتفي الحرج عنه في تحكيمه، ولكن لا ينقاد قلبه ولا يرضى كل الرضى بحكمه. والتسليم أخص من انتفاء الحرج، فالحرج مانع، والتسليم أمر وجودي، ولا يلزم من انتفاء الحرج حصولُ التسليم بمجرد انتفائه، إذ قد ينتفي الحرج ويبقى القلب فارغًا من الرضى به والتسليم له. فتأمله.

وعند هذا يُعلم أن الرب تبارك وتعالى أقسم على انتفاء إيمان أكثر الخلق، وعند الامتحان تعلم هل هذه الأمور الثلاثة موجودة في قلب أكثر من يدعي الإسلام أم لا.

والله المستعان وعليه التكلان ولا حول ولا قوة إلا بالله العلي العظيم.

(فوائد أخرى)

وقد أقسم سبحانه بنفسه المقدسة أنهم لا يؤمنون حتى يحكموا رسوله في كل ما شجر بينهم، ولا يكفي ذلك في حصول الإيمان حتى يزول الحرج من نفوسهم بما حكم به في ذلك أيضًا، حتى يحصل منهم الرضا والتسليم. فقال تعالى ﴿فَلا وَرَبِّكَ لا يُؤْمِنُونَ حَتّى يُحَكِّمُوكَ فِيما شَجَرَ بَيْنَهُمْ ثُمَّ لا يَجِدُوا في أنْفُسِهِمْ حَرَجًا مِمّا قَضَيْتَ ويُسَلِّمُوا تَسْلِيمًا﴾.

فأكد ذلك بضروب من التأكيد:

أحدها: تصدير الجملة المقسم عليها بحرف النفي المتضمن لتأكيد النفي المقسم عليه، وهو في ذلك كتصدير الجملة المثبتة بـ"إنّ".

الثاني: القسم بنفسه سبحانه.

الثالث: أنه أتى بالمقسم عليه بصيغة الفعل الدالة على الحدوث، أي لا يقع منهم إيمان ما حتى يحكموك.

الرابع: أنه أتى في الغاية بـ"حتى" دون "إلا"، المشعرةِ بأنه لا يوجد الإيمان إلا بعد حصول التحكيم، لأن ما بعد "حتى" يدخل فيما قبلها.

الخامس: أنه أتى بالمحكَّم فيه بصيغة الموصول الدالة على العموم، وهو قوله ﴿فِيما شَجَرَ بَيْنَهُمْ﴾، أي في جميع ما تنازعوا فيه من الدقيق والجليل.

السادس: أنه ضم إلى ذلك انتفاء الحرج، وهو الضيق من حكمه.

السابع: أنه أتى به نكرةً في سياق النفي، أي لا يجدون نوعًا من أنواع الحرج البتة.

الثامن: أنه أتى بذكر ما قُضي به بصيغة العموم، فإنها إما مصدرية، أي من قضائك، أو موصولة، أي من الذي قضيته، وهذا يتناول كل فرد من أفراد قضائه.

التاسع: أنه لم يكتفِ منهم بذلك حتى يضيفوا إليه التسليم، وهو قدر زائد على التحكيم وانتفاء الحرج، فما كل من حُكِّم انتفى عنه الحرج، ولا كل من انتفى عنه الحرج يكون مسلِّمًا منقادًا، فإن التسليم يتضمن الرضا بحكمه والانقياد له.

العاشر: أنه أكد فعل التسليم بالمصدر المؤكِّد. ونحن نناشد هؤلاء الجهمية (Jahmiyya) بالله الذي لا إله إلا هو: هل يجدون في أنفسهم هذا التسليم والانقياد والتحكيم للنصوص؟ وهل هم مع الرسول وما جاء به بهذه المنزلة؟ فوالله إن قلوبهم وألسنتهم وكتبهم لتشهد عليهم بضد ذلك، كما يشهد به عليهم المؤمنون والملائكة وأولو العلم، والله سبحانه وكفى بالله شهيدًا.

(فصل)

ومِن مَنازلِ ﴿إيّاكَ نَعْبُدُ وإيّاكَ نَسْتَعِينُ﴾: (مَنزِلَةُ التَّسْلِيمِ)

وهي نوعان: تسليمٌ لحكمه الدينيِّ الأمريِّ، وتسليمٌ لحكمه الكونيِّ القدريِّ.

فأما الأول: فهو تسليمُ المؤمنين العارفين. قال تعالى: ﴿فَلا وَرَبِّكَ لا يُؤْمِنُونَ حَتّى يُحَكِّمُوكَ فِيما شَجَرَ بَيْنَهُمْ ثُمَّ لا يَجِدُوا في أنْفُسِهِمْ حَرَجًا مِمّا قَضَيْتَ ويُسَلِّمُوا تَسْلِيمًا﴾.

فهذه ثلاث مراتب: التحكيم، وسعةُ الصدر بانتفاء الحرج، والتسليم.

وأما التسليم للحكم الكوني: فمَزَلَّةُ أقدامٍ، ومَضَلَّةُ أفهامٍ، حيَّر الأنامَ، وأوقع الخصامَ، وهي مسألةُ الرضا بالقضاء (al-rida bi al-qada')، وقد تقدم الكلام عليها بما فيه كفاية. وبيّنّا أن التسليم للقضاء يُحمد إذا لم يُؤمر العبد بمنازعته ودفعه، ولم يقدر على ذلك، كالمصائب التي لا قدرة له على دفعها.

وأما الأحكام التي أُمر بدفعها: فلا يجوز له التسليم إليها، بل العبودية: مدافعتُها بأحكامٍ أُخَرَ أحبُّ إلى الله منها.

[فصلٌ: التسليم الصادر عن الرضا والاختيار]

قال صاحب "المنازل":

وفي التسليم والثقة والتفويض ما في التوكل من العلل، وهو من أعلى درجات سُبُل العامة.

يعني أن العلل التي في التوكل من معاني الدعوى، ونسبتِه الشيءَ إلى نفسه أولًا، حيث زعم أنه وكّل ربَّه فيه، وتوكّل عليه فيه، وجعله وكيله القائمَ عنه بمصالحه التي كان يحصّلها لنفسه بالأسباب والتصرفات، وغير ذلك من العلل المتقدمة. وقد عرفتَ ما في ذلك.

وليس في التسليم إلا علةٌ واحدة: وهي أن لا يكون تسليمه صادرًا عن محضِ الرضا والاختيار، بل يشوبه كُرهٌ وانقباض، فيسلّم على نوع إغماض. فهذه علة التسليم المؤثرة، فاجتهد في الخلاص منها.

وإنما كان للعامة عنده، لأن الخاصة في شغلٍ عنه باستغراقهم بالفناء في عين الجمع، وجعلُ الفناء غايةَ الاستغراق في عين الجمع هو الذي أوجب ما أوجب، والله المستعان.

(Benefit: the precedence of the Prophets over the Truthful)

As for the precedence of the Prophets over the truthful (al-siddiqun), it is because the truthful one follows the Prophet (ﷺ).

He deserves the name "truthful" only by the perfection of his affirmation of the Prophet, so he is a pure follower.

And reflect on the precedence of the truthful over the martyrs (al-shuhada'), because of the superiority of the truthful over them, and the precedence of the martyrs over the righteous (al-salihun), because of their superiority over them.

(Benefit: the precedence of the Prophets over the Truthful)

As for the precedence of the Prophets over the truthful (al-siddiqun), it is because the truthful one follows the Prophet (ﷺ).

He deserves the name "truthful" only by the perfection of his affirmation of the Prophet, so he is a pure follower.

And reflect on the precedence of the truthful over the martyrs (al-shuhada'), because of the superiority of the truthful over them, and the precedence of the martyrs over the righteous (al-salihun), because of their superiority over them.

(Benefit)

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: The enjoyment of this world is little, and the Hereafter is better for those who fear God, and you will not be wronged the least bit.﴾ It combines discouraging attachment to this world, encouraging desire for the Hereafter, urging the doing of good, and restraining from the doing of evil, since His saying ﴿and you will not be wronged the least bit﴾ includes urging them to earn good and restraining them from earning evil.

(Admonition)

Whoever loves this world, it looks upon his value in its eyes and so makes him one of its servants and slaves, and humiliates him.

And whoever turns away from it, it looks upon the greatness of his worth, so it serves him and submits to him.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 4, verse 79 (part 1 of 4):**

So the *ḥasanah* (good) and the *sayyi'ah* (bad) here mean blessing and affliction. The blessing comes from Allah, Who bestows it upon you as a favour. The affliction arises only from your own self and your own deeds. The first is His bounty (*fadl*) and the second is His justice (*'adl*). The servant moves between His bounty and His justice. His bounty flows over him, His judgment takes effect in him, and His decree is just.

**(Section)**

Here, by *ḥasanah* and *sayyi'ah* is meant the blessings and the calamities that befall the servant from Allah. For this reason He said ﴿what befalls you﴾ and did not say ﴿what you did﴾.

Every deficiency, trial and evil in this world and the Hereafter has as its cause sins and the disobedience of the Lord's commands. There is no evil in the world at all except sins and what necessitates them.

The effects of good and bad deeds on hearts, bodies and wealth are a matter witnessed in the world, which no one of sound intellect denies. Indeed, the believer and the unbeliever, the righteous and the wicked, all know it.

The servant's witnessing of this in himself and in others, and his reflection upon and contemplation of it, strengthens his faith in what the Messengers brought, and in reward and punishment. This is because it is a justice that is witnessed and perceived in this world, and swift rewards and punishments that point to what is greater than them, for whoever has insight. As one of the people said: "When a sin proceeds from me and I do not hasten to it or remedy it with repentance, I await its evil effect. When it befalls me, or something greater or lesser than it, just as I had reckoned, my constant utterance becomes: 'I bear witness that there is no deity but Allah, and I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah.' This is one of the evidences and proofs of faith. For when a truthful one informs you that if you do such and such, a certain hardship will follow from it, and every time you do one of these things the hardship he described befalls you, you do not increase except in knowledge of his truthfulness and insight into it." This is not so for everyone. Rather, most people have sins covering their hearts, so they witness none of this and do not perceive it at all.

This heart in which there is the light of faith, while the winds of sins and disobedience blow upon it, witnesses both this and that. It sees the state of the lamp of its faith amid the strength of those winds and gales. It sees itself like the rider of the sea when the winds rage and the ship tosses and capsizes, especially if it is shattered and he remains on a plank tossed about by the winds. Likewise the believer sees himself when committing sins, if good is intended for him. And if something other than that is intended for him, his heart is in another valley.

When this door is opened for the servant, he benefits from studying the history of the world, the conditions of nations, and the events of creation. Indeed, he benefits from the events of the people of his own time and from what he witnesses of the conditions of people. Then he understands the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then is He who stands over every soul in what it has earned [like those who have no partners]?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 33], and His saying: ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no deity except Him, and the angels and those of knowledge [also testify], standing in justice. There is no deity except Him, the Almighty, the Wise﴾ [Al 'Imran: 18]. So whatever you see in existence of evil, pain, punishment, drought and deficiency, in yourself or in others, it is from the Lord's standing by justice, exalted is He. It is Allah's justice and equity, even if He executes it through the hand of a wrongdoer. The one who empowers him is the Most Just of the just, as He, exalted is He, said to those who spread corruption on earth: ﴿We sent against you servants of Ours of great might, and they ransacked the homes﴾ [al-Isra': 5], and so on.

Sins are like poisons: harmful in themselves. If one remedies them by administering the antidotes that counter them, well and good; otherwise they overcome the power of faith, and destruction follows. As one of the Salaf said: "Sins are the messenger of disbelief, just as fever is the messenger of death."

So the servant's witnessing of the deterioration of his state when he disobeys his Lord, the change of hearts toward him, their recoiling from him, the closing of doors in his face, the difficulty of paths for him, his humiliation before his family, his children, his wife and his brothers, and his seeking to understand all this until he knows from where he was struck, and his discovery of the cause that necessitated it, strengthens his faith. If he then desists and takes up the means that lead to the opposite of this state, he sees might after humiliation, wealth after poverty, joy after sorrow, safety after fear, and strength in his heart after weakness and feebleness. His faith increases upon his faith. Thus the signs of faith in his heart are strengthened, and its proofs and evidences, in his state of disobedience and in his state of obedience. This is among those of whom Allah said: ﴿That Allah may remove from them the worst of what they did and reward them their best of what they used to do﴾ [al-Zumar: 35].

Whoever occupies this station and reflects upon it, giving it its due, becomes one of the physicians of hearts who know their diseases and their remedies. Allah benefits him in his own self, and benefits through him whom He wills of His creatures. And Allah knows best.

**(Benefit)**

As for ﴿Sufficient is Allah as a witness﴾, the *bā'* (ب) is connected to what the statement implies of the meaning of a command to be content. For when you say *kafā billāhi* ("sufficient is Allah") or *kafāka Allāhu Zaydan* ("Allah suffices you, Zayd"), you intend that he be content with Him. So the wording is that of a statement, but the meaning is that of a command. The *bā'* enters for this reason. It is therefore not truly superfluous, but is like your saying *ḥasbuka bi-Zayd* ("Zayd is enough for you"). Do you not see that *ḥasbuka* is a subject (*mubtada'*) and has a predicate, and that with Allah the verb may be jussive (*majzūm*) in its response? You say *ḥasbuka yanam al-nās* ("let the people sleep enough for you"), where *yanam* is in the jussive form as a response to the command implicit in the sentence. Sibawayh related this from the Arabs.

**(Section)**

What further clarifies this matter is that when He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾, He followed it with His saying: ﴿And We have sent you to the people as a messenger, and sufficient is Allah as a witness﴾.

This includes several things. Among them is an alert to His community that if His Messenger, to whom He bore witness of prophethood, is struck by what he dislikes, it is from his own self, so what is to be thought of anyone else?

Among them is that the proof of Allah has been established against them by sending him. So if He, glorified is He, afflicts them with what distresses them, He is not unjust to them in that, since He has sent His Messenger to them to inform them of what is in their interest, what brings it to them, what is harmful to them, and what brings that harm upon them. Whoever finds good should praise Allah, and whoever finds otherwise should blame none but himself.

Among them is that He, glorified is He, has borne witness to his prophethood through the signs He manifested at his hands, which demonstrate his truthfulness and that he is truly His Messenger. So the denial of these ignorant, wrongdoing people who consider him an omen for his message does not harm him, for whom the Lord of the heavens and the earth has borne witness.

Among them is that they wanted to make their own evil deeds and their punishments a proof against the invalidation of his message. So He bore witness to his prophethood and informed them that His witness is sufficient. Thus within this is the refutation of their claim that calamities are from the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the affirmation, by a stronger argument, that they are from themselves.

Among them is the refutation of the statement of the Jahmiyya, the compulsionists (*mujbira*), and those who agree with them in saying that Allah may punish servants without any sin.

Among them is the refutation of the statement of the Qadariyya, who say that the causes of good and bad deeds are not from Allah but from the servant.

Among them is the condemnation of one who does not reflect upon the Qur'an and does not understand it, and that his turning away from its reflection and understanding entails for him misguidance and wretchedness in proportion to his turning away.

Among them is the affirmation of causes and the refutation of the statement of one who denies them and sees no connection between them and their effects.

Among them is that all good is from Allah and all evil is from the self, for evil is sins and their punishment, and sins are from the self while their punishments follow from them. Allah is the One who decreed and ordained that, and everything is with Him by decree and destiny, even if the servant's self is its cause. This is unlike good and blessings, whose cause is purely the bounty, favour and enabling of Allah, as has been established above.

Among them is that when He, glorified is He, rejected their claim that the good is from Allah and the bad is from His Messenger, refuting it with His saying: ﴿Say: all is from Allah﴾, He removed the illusion of one who imagined that the self has no influence on evil and is not its source at all, by His saying: ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾. He addressed this to the Prophet as a warning to others, as has been mentioned.

Among them is that in His rebuttal of them He said: ﴿Say: all is from Allah﴾ and did not say "from Allah" alone, because He combined the good and the bad. The good is attributed to Allah in every respect, whereas the bad is attributed to Him only by way of decree, destiny and creation, in that He is its creator just as He is the creator of the good. Hence He said: ﴿Say: all is from Allah﴾. He, glorified is He, created it for a wisdom, so it is not attributed to Him in terms of its being evil, but in terms of what it contains of wisdom, justice and praiseworthiness, while it is attributed to the self in terms of its being evil.

When He mentioned the good separately from the bad, He said: ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from Allah﴾, and did not say "from the presence of Allah", so the good is from Him and is the requirement of His names and attributes. As for the bad, which is evil in relation to the servant, it is from His presence, glorified is He, since it is created by Him out of justice and wisdom. Then He said: ﴿And whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾, and did not say "from your presence," because the self's nature and disposition require it. So it is from the self, while the whole is from Allah. Thus the evil is from the human self without doubt, and the good is from Allah without doubt, and both are from His presence, glorified is He, by decree, destiny and creation. He distinguishes between what is *min Allah* ("from Allah") and what is *min 'indihi* ("from His presence"). Evil is not attributed to Allah by will, love, action, description or name. He wills only good, loves only good, does no evil, is not described by it, and is not named by it. We shall mention, in the chapter on the entry of evil into the divine decree, the manner in which it is ascribed to His decree and destiny, if Allah wills.

**(Section)**

The Qadari said: Allah, glorified is He, said: ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾.

The Jabari said: All is the action of Allah, and nothing is from the servant.

The Jabari said: There is an implied interrogative in the speech, its meaning being "Is it from your self?" It is a denial, not an affirmation. Some of them read *fa-min nafsika* with a fatḥah on the *mīm* and a ḍammah on *nafsuka*, meaning "who are you that you should do it?" He said: there must be an interpretation of the verse, otherwise it contradicts His statement in the verse before it: ﴿And if a good thing befalls them, they say, "This is from Allah," and if an evil thing befalls them, they say, "This is from you." Say: all is from Allah﴾. So He informed that good and evil are all from His presence, not from the servant's presence.

The Sunni said: You both erred most grievously in understanding the verse. The source of your error is that the good and the evil in the verse are meant as the obedience and disobedience which are the servant's voluntary action. This is pure delusion regarding the verse. What is meant by them is blessings and calamities. The words *ḥasanāt* and *sayyi'āt* in the Book of Allah are sometimes used to mean this and sometimes that. So His saying: ﴿If good touches you, it distresses them, and if an evil afflicts you, they rejoice at it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 120]; and His saying: ﴿If good befalls you, it grieves them, and if a calamity strikes you, they say, "We had already taken our precaution before"﴾ [al-Tawbah: 50]; and His saying: ﴿And We tested them with good and evil﴾ [al-A'raf: 168]; and His saying: ﴿And if an evil befalls them for what their hands have put forth, then indeed man is ungrateful﴾ [al-Shura: 48]; and His saying: ﴿But when good came to them, they said, "This is ours." And if evil afflicted them, they ascribed it to an omen of Moses and those with him﴾ [al-A'raf: 131]; and His saying: ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾. In all of these, what is meant is blessings and calamities. As for His saying: ﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have ten times its like, and whoever brings an evil deed will not be recompensed except by its equivalent﴾ [al-An'am: 160]; and His saying: ﴿Indeed, good deeds remove bad deeds﴾ [Hud: 114]; and His saying: ﴿Those, Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds﴾ [al-Furqan: 70], in all of these what is meant is the commanded and forbidden actions.

He, glorified is He, said "what befalls you" and did not say "what you did and earned." For what the servant does is described with *aṣabta* ("you obtained"), *kasabta* ("you earned") and *'amilta* ("you did"), as in His saying: ﴿And whoever does righteous deeds while he is a believer﴾ [Ta-Ha: 112]; His saying: ﴿Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾ [al-Nisa': 123]; and His saying: ﴿And whoever earns a sin or a wrong﴾ [al-Nisa': 112]. The repentant sinner's statement, "O Messenger of Allah, I have committed a sin, so establish upon me the Book of Allah," is also of this kind. But one does not say "a sin befell you" or "an evil befell you" in this sense. What happens to one without his choice is described with *aṣāba* ("befell"), as in His saying: ﴿And whatever calamity strikes you is for what your hands have earned﴾ [al-Shura: 30]; His saying: ﴿And if a calamity strikes you, they say, "We had already taken our precaution before"﴾ [al-Tawbah: 50]; and His saying: ﴿Why, when a calamity struck you, although you had struck [the enemy] with twice as much, did you say, "From where is this?"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 165]. So in this verse He combined what they obtained by their own action and earning, and what befell them that was not their action. And His saying: ﴿And we await for you that Allah will afflict you with punishment from Himself﴾ [al-Tawbah: 52]; His saying: ﴿And the disbelievers will not cease to be struck by a calamity for what they have done﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31]; and His saying: ﴿So the calamity of death struck you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 106]. So His saying: ﴿Whatever good befalls you﴾ is of this category, which the servant suffers without his choice.

This is the consensus of the Salaf in the interpretation of this verse.

Abu al-'Aliyah said: "*And if a good thing befalls them*: this is in ease; *and if an evil befalls them*: this is in hardship."

Al-Suddi said: "The good is fertility, so their livestock and cattle produce young, their condition becomes good, and their women bear sons. They said, 'This is from Allah.' And if an evil befalls them, that is harm to their wealth. They took it as an omen of Muhammad and said, 'This is from him.' They said, 'Because we abandoned our religion and followed Muhammad, what has befallen us has befallen us.' So Allah, glorified is He, sent down, in reply to them: *Say: all is from Allah*, the good and the evil."

Al-Walibi related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding *Whatever good befalls you is from Allah*: "It is what Allah opened for you on the day of Badr." He also said: "It is the spoils and the victory. And the evil is what befell him on the day of Uhud: his face was wounded and his front tooth was broken." He also said: "As for the good, Allah bestowed it upon you; as for the evil, He tested you with it." He also said: "Whatever calamity befalls you is for your sin, and I have decreed it upon you." All of this was related by Ibn Abi Hatim. In the tafsir of Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas: "*If good befalls you*: fertility; *if evil befalls you*: drought and affliction."

Ibn Qutaybah said regarding this verse: "*Ḥasanah* is blessing, and *sayyi'ah* is affliction."

If it is said: Abu al-Faraj Ibn al-Jawzi related from Abu al-'Aliyah that he interpreted *ḥasanah* and *sayyi'ah* in this verse as obedience and disobedience, and he is among the most knowledgeable of the Successors?

The answer is that he did not cite a chain of transmission (isnad) for this, and we do not know it to be authentic from Abu al-'Aliya. Ibn Abi Hatim did cite, through his own chain, a report from Abu al-'Aliya, mentioned earlier, that this refers to ease and hardship (al-sarra' wa al-darra'). This is the well-known view of Abu al-'Aliya, and Ibn Abi Hatim did not report any other view from him. It is also what Ibn Qutayba related from him. It may be said that both meanings are intended, on the basis that whatever obedience (ta'a) God enables a person to perform is a blessing (ni'ma) for him that comes to him from God, as He says: ﴿And whatever blessing you have is from God﴾. This includes the blessings of religion and of worldly life. Whatever sin he commits is a calamity (musiba) that befalls him from God, even though its cause is from him. What makes this clear is that when God, glory be to Him, made the bad outcome (sayyi'a) the recompense for disobedience, by saying from the person's own self: ﴿And whatever misfortune befalls you, it is from yourself﴾, then the deed that made recompense necessary is more fittingly from his own self. There is no contradiction between the bad deed being from one's own self and the bad recompense being from one's own self. Yet this does not preclude that all of it is from God by decree and predestination (qada' wa qadar). Rather, what is from God is justice, wisdom, benefit and goodness, while what is from the servant is a bad and ugly act.

It has been related from Ibn 'Abbas that he used to recite it: ﴿And whatever misfortune befalls you, it is from yourself﴾ and "I have decreed it upon you." This reading is an added clarification. Otherwise, God's earlier statement ﴿Say: all is from God﴾ already indicates the preceding, all-encompassing decree and predestination. Sins may be partly a punishment for other sins, so that God has two punishments for one disobedience: a punishment through a sin that arises from it, where the first is its cause, and a punishment through a painful outcome that is its recompense. This is as in the hadith agreed upon as authentic from Ibn Mas'ud, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Hold fast to truthfulness, for truthfulness leads to righteousness, and righteousness leads to Paradise. A man continues to be truthful and seeks truthfulness until he is recorded with God as a truthful one (siddiq). Beware of lying, for lying leads to wickedness, and wickedness leads to the Fire. A man continues to lie and seeks lying until he is recorded with God as a liar (kadhdhab)."

God, glory be to Him, has mentioned in more than one place in His Book that a good deed may be a reward for an earlier good deed, and that a sin may be a punishment for an earlier sin. The first is as in His saying: ﴿And if they had done what they were admonished with, it would have been better for them and firmer in confirmation. And then We would have given them from Us a great reward, and We would have guided them to a straight path﴾. He also says: ﴿And those who strive for Us, We will surely guide them to Our ways﴾, and: ﴿By it God guides whoever follows His pleasure to the ways of peace and brings them out of darknesses into light by His permission and guides them to a straight path﴾.

As for His saying: ﴿And those who are killed in the way of God—He will never allow their deeds to be lost. He will guide them and amend their condition﴾, it may be that this is not of this type, and that the guidance is in the Hereafter, to the path of Paradise, since He has made this reward follow their being killed. It may also be that it is of this type, and that His saying ﴿He will guide them and amend their condition﴾ is an announcement from Him, glory be to Him, of what He does for those who were killed in His way before they were killed, and it is expressed in the future tense to inform that He renews for them, at every moment, a kind of guidance and the amending of their condition, one after another. If you say: how can that future tense be a report about those who were killed? I say: the predicate is His saying ﴿He will never allow their deeds to be lost﴾, meaning that He does not nullify them for them nor deprive them of them. This is after they were killed. Then God, glory be to Him, gives a separate report about them that He will guide them and amend their condition, since He knew that they would be killed in His way and that they had given themselves up for Him. So for them there are two rewards: a reward in this world through guidance for their striving, and a reward in the Hereafter through entering Paradise. The listener therefore returns each clause to its proper time, since the meaning is clear and not ambiguous. This is common in the Qur'an, and God knows best.

God also says: ﴿Thus, that We might turn away from him evil and immorality﴾; and: ﴿And when he reached his maturity and became fully grown, We gave him judgment and knowledge. And thus do We reward the doers of good﴾; and: ﴿O you who have believed, fear God and speak words of appropriate justice; He will amend for you your deeds and forgive you your sins﴾; and: ﴿And if you obey him, you will be guided﴾; and: ﴿Then We gave Moses the Book, complete, upon the one who did good﴾. Here "tamam" (completion) is taken to imply the meaning of "in'am" (bestowal), so it is followed by "'ala" (upon), meaning: as a bestowal from Us upon the one who did good. This is a recompense for good deeds with good deeds.

As for recompense for sins with sins, it is like His saying: ﴿So when they deviated, God caused their hearts to deviate﴾; His saying: ﴿And do not be like those who forgot God, so He caused them to forget themselves﴾; His saying: ﴿And We turn their hearts and their sight away, as they did not believe in it the first time, and We leave them in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾; His saying: ﴿Indeed, those of you who turned back on the day the two armies met—Satan only caused them to slip because of some of what they had earned﴾; His saying: ﴿And they say: "Our hearts are closed." Rather, God has cursed them for their disbelief, so little is it that they believe﴾; and His saying: ﴿And on the day of Hunayn, when your large numbers pleased you but gave you no benefit at all, and the earth was confining for you in spite of its vastness, and you turned back retreating﴾. This is abundant in the Qur'an.

On this basis, the two types of evil, namely calamities and faults, are from the human self, and both are by God's decree. The evil of the self is what caused this and that. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to say in his well-known sermon: "And we seek refuge with God from the evils of our souls and from the bad outcomes of our deeds." The evil of the self is of two kinds: a quality (sifa) and an action ('amal). The action arises from the quality, and the quality is strengthened and confirmed by the action, so each feeds the other. The bad deeds are of two kinds, as the hadith explains. One is their faults and ugliness, so the attribution (idafa) in it is from the kind to its genus, meaning "of" (min): the bad deeds of our actions. The second is that they are what harms the doer of the outcome of his deeds, so it is the attribution of the effect to its cause, and the attribution carries the sense of "for" (li). It may be preferred that the first meaning is intended, since he sought refuge from the quality and the action arising from it, and that includes seeking refuge from the bad recompense that follows. Thus the seeking of refuge includes three things: seeking refuge from the punishment, from its cause which is the action, and from the cause of the action which is the quality. It may also be preferred that the second meaning is intended, since the evil of the self encompasses both kinds, as stated before. The bad outcomes of deeds are what harms in recompense. By his saying "the bad deeds of our actions," he indicates that what harms in recompense is only because of voluntary actions, not because of qualities which are not our actions. Since that quality was an evil, he sought refuge from it and included it within the evil of the self.

Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may God be pleased with him, said: "O Messenger of God, teach me a supplication to make in my prayer." He said: "Say: O God, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, Lord and Sovereign of everything, I bear witness that there is no god but You. I seek refuge with You from the evil of my self, the evil of Satan and his association, and that I commit against myself an evil or bring it upon a Muslim." Say it when you rise in the morning, when you enter the evening, and when you lie down on your bed.

Since evil has a source from which it begins and an end to which it reaches, and its source is either from the human self, or from Satan, and its end is that it returns upon its owner or upon his Muslim brother, the supplication comprises these four levels in the most concise, clearest and most explicit wording.

(Section)

The Sunni said: O Qadari, you cannot argue for your doctrine from the verse we are discussing, for several reasons.

First: you say that the act of the servant, whether good or bad, is from him and not from God. God, glory be to Him, has given each one the capacity (istita'a) by which to do good and evil. But this one initiated by his own will the intention to do good deeds, and that one initiated the intention to do evil deeds. Neither of the two intentions is from the Lord, glory be to Him, in any way, nor did His will necessitate them. The verse distinguishes between good and bad, while you do not distinguish between them, for God, according to you, did not will this or that.

The Qadari said: It is attributed to the servant's self because he is the one who brought it into being and created it, and the good is attributed to Him, glory be to Him, because He is the one who commanded it and legislated it.

The Sunni said: God, glory be to Him, attributed to the servant the evil that befell him, and attributed to Himself the good that befell the servant. It is known that what befell the servant is what subsisted in him, and the command did not subsist in the servant; rather, what subsisted in him was the one commanded, and it is that which befell him. So what befell him cannot, according to you, be attributed to the Lord. What is attributed to the Lord did not subsist in the servant. Therefore it is known that what befell him, in this case and that, is a matter subsisting in him. If what was meant were voluntary acts of obedience and disobedience, the attribution would be equal and no distinction would be valid, even though they differ in that one is commanded and the other forbidden. Moreover, the prohibition is also from God, just as the command is from Him. If the attribution were due to the command, then the commanded and the forbidden would be equal in attribution, since the one is required to be brought into being and the other is required to be annihilated.

The Qadari said: I permit that obedience and disobedience are connected to the will of the Lord, glory be to Him, and to His bringing them about as a recompense, not as a beginning. God, glory be to Him, punishes His servant with what He wills and rewards him. Just as He punishes him by creating the recompense that displeases him, and creates the reward that pleases him, so it is fitting that He punishes him by creating disobedience and creating obedience. This would be just from Him. But that He should create in him disbelief and disobedience as a beginning, without cause, God forbid.

The Sunni said: This is an excellent middle position, which neither reason nor revelation rejects. But whoever initiates the first (act), and it is not, according to you, something decreed by God or occurring by His will, has then asserted in His dominion what He is not able to do and admitted into it what He does not will. You have overturned your entire principle, for you established that the voluntary act of the servant is his power and his choice, and that his will prevents the Lord's power over it and His will for it. This principle makes no distinction between the initiating and the recompensing act.

The Qadari said: The Qur'an distinguishes between the two kinds and makes disbelief and wickedness the second as a recompense for the first, so it is known that the first is from the servant with certainty; otherwise it would not be proper to make one a punishment for the other. He has stated this explicitly in His saying: ﴿So for their breaking of their covenant, We cursed them and made their hearts hard﴾. Here He attributed the breaking of the covenant to them and the hardening of hearts to Himself. The first is from them as a cause, and the second is from Him, glory be to Him, as a recompense. He says: ﴿And We turn their hearts and their sight away, as they did not believe in it the first time, and We leave them in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾. Here He attributed the non-belief at first to them, since it is the cause, and the turning of hearts and the leaving them in their transgression is the recompense. Similarly, His saying: ﴿So when they deviated, God caused their hearts to deviate﴾. The verses you have just heard point to this.

The Sunni said: Yes, this is true, but it does not remove the cause from being within the Lord's power and occurring by His will. If He willed, He could have placed a barrier between the servant and it, and guided him to its opposite. This is the remnant that remains on you from the doctrine of qadar, just as denying the establishment of causes and their necessary consequences and their ordering is the remnant that remains on the Jabari (determinist) in this question. Each of you is right in one respect and wrong in another. If each of you freed himself from the remnant that remained on him, you would both find the spirit of agreement and unite upon the truth. And success is from God.

The Qadari said: What do you say, O Sunni, about the first act if it is not a recompense? What is its reason? You are one who holds to wisdom and causation, and who exalts the Lord, glory be to Him, above injustice, which is injustice, not what the Jabari says, that it is the combining of two contradictories.

The Sunni said: It is not incumbent on me in this position to explain that, for I have not set myself up to do so. I have only set myself up to refute your argument from the verse for your false doctrine, and I have fulfilled that. God has wisdoms and praiseworthy ends in this that the minds of the intelligent and the insights of the clever cannot reach. God, glory be to Him, places His favor, His guidance and His support in the place that is suited to it, and what is unsuited He leaves empty and devoid of guidance and success, so it follows its nature upon which it was created: ﴿And if God had known any good in them, He would have made them hear. And if He had made them hear, they would have turned away while being averse﴾.

The Qadari said: If God has produced in them that will and intention which necessarily entails the existence of the act, then that is His bringing that into being in them, just as He brought guidance and faith into being in those who deserve them.

The Sunni said: This is the battlefield of contention, and the point where the paths of the world diverge. God, glory be to Him, gave the servant an intention, a power and a will suitable for this and for that. Then He strengthened those of virtue with additional existential means beyond that common endowment, which made guidance and faith necessary for them, and He withheld that strengthening from whom He knew was not suited to it and not fitting for it. So the powers of his will and intention turned toward the opposite, by his own choice and love, not by compulsion or necessity.

The Qadari said: Was it possible for him to will what he was not helped to and not enabled to do by an additional strengthening beyond the creation of the will?

The Sunni said: If by possibility you mean that it is possible for him to do it if he willed, then yes, it is possible in this sense, and it is within his power. But if you mean that its occurrence is possible without the will and permission of the Lord, then it is not possible. For what God wills comes to be and becomes necessary, and what He does not will does not come to be and its existence is impossible.

The Qadari said: Then you concede that it is not possible for the servant if God does not will him to do it, so it is no longer within the servant's power, and he is punished for abandoning what he is unable to do.

The Sunni said: God's not willing for the servant and not intending that he do it does not necessitate that the act be outside his power. For God, glory be to Him, does not will for Himself to assist him in it while having enabled him to do it, and it does not follow from His enabling him that it occurs unless another assistance is granted. The absence of that assistance does not remove the act from being within the servant's power. He may be able to do the act but abandon it out of laziness and negligence, preferring its opposite. God does not turn away from him the abandonment that occurs, and the absence of turning away does not make him incapable of the act. God, glory be to Him, knows that he is able to do it by the power with which He enabled him, and He knows that He does not will it for him even though he is able to do it. So He, glory be to Him, wills it, and the act is from Him, but He does not will to assist and enable him to do it from Himself. The cutting off of this assistance and enabling does not remove the act from being within his power, even if you make it not willed. The secret of the question is the distinction between the will's relation to the act of the servant and its relation to His own act after it. Whoever has not fully grasped this distinction has not had the veil of the question lifted from him.

The Jabari said: As for whether you say that God knew the servant would not act, or did not know that, the second is impossible. If He knew that he would not do it, the act becomes absolutely impossible, for if he did it, the eternal knowledge would turn into ignorance.

The Sunni said: This is a false argument from several aspects. The first is that this very same thing can be said about what God knows the servant will not do, though it is within his power, for it is of no benefit whatsoever even though it is within his power. So whatever your answer is to that, it is our answer to you. The second is that God, glory be to Him, knows things as they are, so He knows that he will not do it because He does not will it, not because He is unable to do it. The third is that knowledge is revelatory, not determinative; the determining factor is the will of the Lord, and knowledge reveals the realities of the things known.

We return to the discussion of the verse which the Qadari used as an argument, and to showing that there is no proof in it from three aspects. The first is that He said "what befalls you" and did not say "what you have done." The second is that by good and evil is meant blessing and calamity. The third is that He said: ﴿Say: all is from God﴾. The human being is the doer of evil deeds and deserves punishment for them, while God is the one who bestows blessings upon him by deeds and by recompense, and who justly brings evils upon him by decree and recompense. If good deeds were from the servant's self just as bad deeds are from his self, then both would be from his self, yet God, glory be to Him, has distinguished between the two kinds. In the authentic divine hadith: "O My servants, it is only your deeds that I count for you, then I repay you for them in full. Whoever finds good, let him praise God, and whoever finds otherwise, let him blame no one but himself."

(Section)

The Jabari said: The beginning of the verse is clear (muhkam), namely His saying ﴿all is from God﴾, and its end is ambiguous (mutashabih), namely His saying: ﴿What good befalls you is from God, and what evil befalls you is from yourself﴾.

The Qadari said: Its end is clear and its beginning is ambiguous?

Al-Sunni said: You have both erred. Rather, both (statements) are muhkam and clear. You only came to this because of your lack of understanding of the Qur'an and of reflecting upon it. There is no contradiction between the two expressions, neither in meaning nor in wording. For He, glorified and exalted, mentioned of these who shirk from jihad that when good befalls them they say, "This is from Allah," and when evil befalls them they say to His Messenger ﷺ, "This is from you," meaning: because of what you commanded us of your religion and our abandoning what we were upon, these evils have struck us, for you commanded us with that which necessitated them. So "evils" here are the calamities, and the deeds which they thought were the cause of the calamities are those they were commanded to do. Their saying about the evil that befalls them, "This is from you," encompasses the calamities of jihad that befell them, such as defeat, wounds, and the killing of some of them, and it also encompasses calamities of provision in the manner of tatayyur (omen-taking) and tashaʾum (ill-omen), meaning: this has struck us because of your religion, as He, exalted, said about the people of Pharaoh: ﴿But when good came to them, they said, "This is ours," and if evil afflicted them, they ascribed it to omen from Moses and those with him﴾. That is, when there came to them what gladdened them and what they enjoyed of blessings, they said, "We are the people of this and deserve it," and if what displeased them afflicted them, they said, "This is because of what Moses brought." And the people of the town said to the messengers, "Indeed we see an omen in you." And the people of Salih, peace be upon him, said, "We see an omen in you and in those with you." They used to say, regarding what befell them from the cause of war, "This is from you," because you commanded us with the deeds that necessitate it, and the calamities that occurred from a direction other than the enemy. "And this too is from you," meaning: because of our separation from our religion and the religion of our forefathers and our entry into your obedience. This is the state of everyone who makes obedience to the Messenger ﷺ a cause of evil that befalls him, whether from the heavens or from the earth. Such people are many among mankind, and they are the least in rank with Allah, the most despicable in His sight. It is well known that they did not say, "This is from you" in the sense of "you invented it." Whoever understands this will see clearly that His saying: ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾ does not contradict His saying: ﴿Say, "All is from Allah"﴾; rather, it is a confirmation of it. For He, glorified, made clear that blessings and calamities are all from Him. He is the Creator of them, the One who decrees them, and the One who tests His creation with them. So they are from Him; none of them is from Him while another part is created by someone else. How then could some of them be attributed to the Messenger ﷺ and some to Allah, exalted? It is well known that the Messenger ﷺ did not bring them into being. So nothing remains except their supposition that he is a cause of their occurrence, either in general, as with the people of tatayyur, or in a specific event, as with those who blamed him concerning jihad. Allah, glorified, nullified that false delusion and baseless supposition, and made clear that what he brought does not necessitate evil at all; rather, all good is in what he ﷺ brought, and evil is due to their deeds and sins, as the messengers, peace be upon them, said to the people of the town: ﴿Your omen is with you﴾. This is not contradicted by the saying of Salih, peace be upon him, to his people: ﴿Your omen is with Allah﴾, nor by His saying about the people of Pharaoh: ﴿And if evil afflicted them, they ascribed it to omen from Moses and those with him. Surely their omen is with Allah﴾. Rather, these two attributions are a parallel of these two attributions in this verse: the attribution of evil to the servant's own self, and the attribution of good and evil to being from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. So reflect upon the harmony of the Qur'an and how its parts confirm one another. Where He made the omen "with them" and the evil "from their own selves," it is in the sense of cause and necessitation, i.e., the evil and ill-omen that struck you is from you, and its causes are established in you, just as you say, "Your evil is from you and your ill-omen is in you," meaning the deed. "Your omen is with you" means the deed. And where He made all of that from Him, it is because He is the Creator of it and the One who recompenses for it with justice and wisdom. So "omen" here refers to the deed and its recompense: what is attributed to the servant is the deed, and what is attributed to the Lord is the recompense. Thus, "your omen is with you" is the omen of the deed, and "your omen is with Allah" is the recompense. What the messengers brought is not a cause of any calamity, and obedience to Allah and His Messenger is never a cause of misfortune. Rather, obedience to Allah and His Messenger brings nothing but good in this world and the Hereafter. But believers in Allah and His Messenger may be afflicted with calamities because of their sins and their shortcomings in obeying Allah and His Messenger, as happened to them on the day of Uhud and the day of Hunayn. Likewise, what they were tested with of adversity and the harm of the disbelievers toward them is not due to the very essence of their faith, nor is it its necessary consequence; rather, they were tested with it so that the evil in them might be separated out, just as gold is tested by fire to separate it from its dross. The souls contain what is part of their natural disposition, so the trial purifies the believer of that which is among the requirements of his nature, as He, exalted, said: ﴿And that Allah may purify those who believe and destroy the disbelievers﴾, and He said: ﴿And that Allah may test what is in your hearts﴾. So obedience to Allah and His Messenger brings nothing but good, and disobedience to them brings nothing but evil. For this reason He, glorified, said: ﴿What is wrong with these people, that they can hardly understand any statement?﴾ For if they had understood the message, they would have known that there is nothing in the message which Allah sent down to His Messenger that necessitates evil at all, and they would have known that it is the cause of all good. Had they understood, they would have known that intellects and natural dispositions bear witness that the interests of this life and the next are tied to what the Messenger brought. Had they comprehended the Qur'an, they would have known that it commands them with every good and forbids them from every evil. This shows that what Allah commands is known to be good by reason, and that it is entirely interest, mercy, benefit and kindness, unlike what many of the people of kalam (theological discourse) falsely say: that He, glorified, commands His servants with what holds no interest for them, rather commands them with what harms them. The saying of these people is a confirmation and an affirmation of the saying of those who ascribed omens to the messengers.

(Section)
Among the things that clarify this matter is that when He, glorified, said: ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾, He followed it with His saying: ﴿And We have sent you to mankind as a Messenger, and Allah suffices as a witness﴾.
This contains several things. Among them: an alert to His community that if His Messenger, whose messengership He testified to, is struck by what he dislikes, it is from his own self, so what then of others? Among them: the proof of Allah has been established against them by his being sent; so when He afflicts them with what displeases them, He is not unjust to them in that, for He has sent His Messenger to them to inform them of what is in their interest and what brings it to them, and what is harmful to them and what brings it to them. Whoever finds good, let him praise Allah; and whoever finds otherwise, let him blame none but himself. Among them: He, glorified, testified to his messengership by the signs He manifested through his hands that show his truthfulness and that he is truly His Messenger; so the denial of these ignorant, wrongdoing people who ascribe omens to him does not harm his messengership, for whoever is testified to by the Lord of the heavens and the earth [is not harmed]. Among them: they wanted to make their evil deeds and their punishments a proof against the nullification of his messengership; so He testified to his messengership and informed that His testimony suffices. Thus, implicit in that is the nullification of their claim that calamities are from the Messenger ﷺ and the affirmation, by even stronger implication, that they are from themselves. Among them: the nullification of the saying of the Jahmiyyah (Jahmites) and the Jabriyyah (determinists) and whoever agrees with them in saying that Allah may punish servants without sin. Among them: the nullification of the saying of the Qadariyyah (predestinarians, i.e., those denying divine decree over human acts) who say that the causes of good and evil deeds are not from Allah but from the servant. Among them: the censure of whoever does not reflect upon the Qur'an and does not understand it, and that his turning away from reflecting upon it and understanding it necessitates for him error and wretchedness in proportion to his turning away. Among them: the affirmation of causes and the nullification of the saying of those who deny them and see no connection between them and their effects. Among them: that all good is from Allah and all evil is from the self, for evil is sins and their punishment, and sins are from the self, and their punishments follow upon them, while Allah is the One who decreed and ordained that, and everything is from Him by decree and predestination, even if the servant's self is its cause. This is unlike good and good deeds, for their cause is purely Allah's bounty, grace, and enabling, as has been established above. Among them: that when He, glorified, rejected their saying that good is from Allah and evil is from His Messenger, and nullified it by His saying: ﴿Say, "All is from Allah"﴾, He removed the delusion of whoever imagined that the self has no influence on evil and is not its source at all, by His saying: ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾, and He addressed him with this as an alert to others, as has been mentioned. Among them: that in His response to them He said: ﴿Say, "All is from Allah"﴾ and did not say "from Allah," because He combined good and evil; good is attributed to Allah in every respect, while evil is attributed to Him only in terms of decree, predestination, and creation, since He is the Creator of it just as He is the Creator of good. Therefore He said: ﴿Say, "All is from Allah"﴾. He, glorified, created it only for a wisdom; so it is not attributed to Him by virtue of being evil, but by virtue of what it contains of wisdom, justice, and praiseworthiness, while being evil is attributed to the self. When He mentioned good separately from evil, He said: ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from Allah﴾ and did not say "from the presence of Allah," for good is from Him and is the requirement of His names and attributes. Evil, which is evil relative to the servant, is from the presence of Allah, since He created it as justice and wisdom from Him. Then He said: ﴿And whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾ and did not say "from your presence," because the self's nature and requirement is that. So it is from the self, and everything is from the presence of Allah. Evil is from the human self without doubt, and good is from Allah without doubt, and both are from His presence by decree, predestination, and creation. Thus, a distinction is made between what is "from Allah" and what is "from His presence," and evil is not attributed to Allah by will, love, action, description, or name, for He wills only good, loves only good, does not do evil, is not described by it, and is not named by it. We will mention, in the chapter on the entry of evil into the divine decree, the manner of its attribution to His decree and predestination, if Allah wills.

(Section)
There has been disagreement concerning the second-person pronoun (kaf al-khitab) in His saying: ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾:
Is it addressed to the Messenger of Allah, or to each individual of the children of Adam?
Ibn ʿAbbas, in the narration of al-Walibi from him, said: "The good is what Allah granted him on the day of Badr of spoils and victory, and the evil is what befell him on the day of Uhud, when his face was wounded and his front tooth was broken."
Another group said: rather, what is meant is the species of the son of Adam, like His saying: ﴿O man, what has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Generous?﴾ Sa'id narrated from Qatadah regarding: ﴿And whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾: he said, "A punishment, O son of Adam, for your sin."
Another group preferred the first view.
They argued with His saying: ﴿And We have sent you to mankind as a Messenger﴾. They said: Moreover, there has been no prior mention of "man" or of addressing him; rather, what preceded was the mention of a group. They said: what Allah relates of them is what is meant, and had they been the intended ones, He would have said "what befell them" or "what befell you" by way of iltifat (shift of address). They said: this is by way of an example (min bab al-sabab), since if the lord of the children of Adam (ﷺ) is like this, how much more so others. Another group preferred the other view.
It argued that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is an infallible scholar from whom nothing proceeds that would necessitate that an evil befall him because of it. They said: the address, though in form to him, is meant for the community, like His saying: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women﴾. They said: since the beginning of the verse was an address to him, the whole address was carried out in one manner, so He made it singular in the second part while meaning all of them. The meaning is: "Whatever evil befalls you is from yourselves"; the first is to him and the second to his community. For this reason, when He made singular the affliction of evil, He said: ﴿And whatever calamity befalls you, it is because of what your hands have earned﴾, and He said: ﴿When a calamity struck you, though you had struck twice as much, you said, "How is this?" Say, "It is from yourselves."﴾ And He said: ﴿And the day of Hunayn, when your large numbers pleased you but they did not avail you at all, and the earth became constricted for you despite its vastness; then you turned back fleeing. Then Allah sent down His tranquility upon His Messenger and upon the believers﴾. Thus He informed that the defeat was due to their sins and their self-admiration, and that the victory was by what He sent down upon His Messenger and strengthened him with, since he did not have any part in the cause of the defeat that they had. A third group combined the two views and said: the form of address is to him ﷺ, while the intended meaning is generality, like His saying: ﴿O Prophet, fear Allah and do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾, then He said: ﴿And follow what is revealed to you from your Lord﴾, then He said: ﴿And rely upon Allah﴾, and like His saying: ﴿And it has certainly been revealed to you and to those before you: If you should associate others with Allah, your deeds would surely become worthless, and you would surely be among the losers. Rather, worship Allah and be among the grateful﴾, and His saying: ﴿So if you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you, then ask those who recite the Scripture before you﴾.
They said: this address is of two kinds. One kind is one whose wording is specific to him, yet it encompasses others by way of a fortiori reasoning, like His saying: ﴿O Prophet, why do you prohibit what Allah has made lawful for you, seeking the approval of your wives?﴾ Then He said: ﴿Allah has already ordained for you the dissolution of your oaths﴾.
And the other kind is one where the address is to him and to the community, but He singled him out for the address because he is the one addressed directly by revelation, the primary recipient of it, the conveyor to the community, and the envoy between them and Allah. This is the meaning of the saying of many exegetes: "The address is to him and the intended meaning is others," and they did not mean by this that he was not addressed at all or that it was not directed at him in any way; rather, the meaning is that since he was the imam of creation, its leader and the one it follows, he was singled out for the address, and the community followed him in its ruling, as a sultan says to the commander of the armies: "March out tomorrow, camp in such-and-such a place, and charge the enemy at such-and-such a time." They said: So His saying: ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾ is an address to him, and the entire community is included in it by way of a fortiori reasoning. This differs from His saying: ﴿And We have sent you to mankind as a Messenger﴾, for that is specific to him. They said: this conditional clause does not necessitate occurrence; it only links the consequent to the condition. As for the occurrence of the condition and the consequent, it does not indicate that. It is hypothetical regarding him, and actual regarding others. And Allah knows best.

Al-Qadari said: If good deeds and sins are decreed, and blessings and calamities are decreed, then why did He, glorified, distinguish between the good deeds, which are blessings, and the evil deeds, which are calamities, making these from Him, glorified, and those from the human self, while all of it is decreed?

Al-Sunni said: There are differences between them. The first difference: Allah's blessings and His kindness toward His servants occur without any acquisition on their part at all. Rather, the Lord, glorified, bestows upon them well-being, provision, victory, the sending of messengers, the sending down of scriptures, and the means of guidance, and He does that without any cause from them that would necessitate it. He creates for Paradise a creation to dwell in it without any cause from them, and He admits the children of believers and their insane ones into Paradise without any deed. As for punishment, He punishes no one except for his deed.

The second difference: performing good deeds is from God's beneficence, bounty and favour toward him, through guidance and faith, as the people of Paradise said: ﴿Praise be to God, who guided us to this. We would never have been guided had God not guided us﴾. The Lord, glory be to Him, created for them life, hearing, sight, minds and hearts; sent the Messengers and their delivery of the message by which they were guided; inspired them to faith; made it beloved to them; adorned it in their hearts; and made its opposite hateful to them. All of this is from His blessings, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿But God has made faith beloved to you and has adorned it in your hearts, and has made disbelief, wickedness and disobedience hateful to you. Those are the rightly guided, a bounty from God and a favour, and God is All-Knowing, All-Wise﴾. Everything that the world turns in, of the good of this life and the Hereafter, is pure blessing, with no prior cause that necessitates it for them, and without any power or strength of their own except through Him. He is their Creator, the Creator of their righteous deeds, and the Creator of their reward. All of this comes from Him, glory be to Him. Evil, by contrast, occurs only through the sins of the servant, and his sin comes from himself.

When the servant reflects on this, he knows that the good he has is from God's grace, so he thanks his Lord for it, and He increases him from His grace with righteous deeds and blessings that He pours upon him. When he knows that evil befalls him only from himself and through his sins, he seeks forgiveness from his Lord and repents, and the cause of evil is removed from him. Thus he is always thankful and seeking forgiveness, and good continues to multiply for him while evil is averted from him. This is как the Prophet (ﷺ) used to say in his sermon: "Praise be to God," thanking God; then he said: "We seek His help and seek His forgiveness. We seek His help in obedience to Him, and we seek His forgiveness for our disobedience, and we praise Him for His deeds and His kindness." Then he said: "And we seek refuge in God from the evils of our souls," so for the sins he had already sought forgiveness, he sought refuge from the sins that had not yet occurred. Then he said: "And from the evil of our deeds," and this is a seeking of refuge from their consequences, as has been mentioned. Then he said: "Whomever God guides, none can misguide; and whomever He misguides, none can guide." This is a testimony to the Lord that He is the one who disposes of His creation by His will, power, wisdom and knowledge, and that He guides whom He wills and misleads whom He wills. When He guides a servant, no one can mislead him, and when He misleads him, no one can guide him. In this is the affirmation of His lordship, power, knowledge, wisdom, decree and divine destiny (qadar), which is the foundation and core of the system of tawhid (the oneness of God). All of this is a preface to His saying: "I bear witness that there is no god but God, and I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger," for the two testimonies are only realised through praising God, seeking His help, seeking His forgiveness, turning to Him for refuge, and believing in His decrees.

The point is that He, glory be to Him, distinguished between good deeds and evil deeds after combining them in His saying: ﴿All is from God﴾. He combined them in the combination without which faith is not complete, which is their being together in His decree, His destiny, His will and His creation. Then He distinguished between them in the distinction from which they benefit: this good and this good deed is a blessing from Him, so thank Him for it, and He will increase you in His grace and blessings; and this evil and this misdeed is because of your sins, so seek His forgiveness and He will lift it from you; and its origin is the evils of your souls, so seek refuge in Him and He will save you from them. This cannot be achieved except by faith in God alone, who guides and misleads, and this is faith in divine destiny (qadar). So enter upon Him through its gate, for the reins of affairs are in His hand. When you do this, your testimony that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God is truthful. This great sermon is the system of Islam and faith. If it had been limited to combining without distinguishing, the disobedient and sinner would turn away from blaming himself, from repenting of his sins, and from seeking refuge from their evil, and the testimony of the argument against his Lord by means of destiny would stand in his heart. That is a false argument, which the wretched followed Iblis in, and it increases its holder only in wretchedness and punishment, just as it increased Iblis in expulsion and distance from his Lord, and just as it increased the polytheists in error and misery when they said: ﴿If God had willed, we would not have associated anything with Him, nor would our fathers﴾. It also increases the one who says on the Day of Resurrection: ﴿If only God had guided me, I would have been among the righteous,﴾ as regret and punishment. If it had been limited to distinguishing without combining, they would have been absorbed by it into tawhid and faith in destiny, and into turning to God for guidance and success, seeking refuge in Him from the evil of the self and the evils of deeds, and into complete need for His help and grace. In combining and distinguishing there is the clarification of the right of servitude (ubudiyya).

The complete discussion of this most important point regarding destiny will come, God willing, by establishing the coming-together and the separation of destiny and the revealed law (shari'ah).

The third difference: God, glory be to Him, multiplies the good deed, increases it, and records it for the servant with little effort, and rewards him for the mere intention to do it. The evil deed is not counted against him for merely intending it, and it is not multiplied; it is erased by repentance. Good deeds erase sins, and afflictions expiate them. Therefore the good deed is more appropriate to be attributed to Him, exalted is He, and the evil deed is more appropriate to be attributed to the self.

The fourth difference: the good deed, which is obedience and blessing, He loves and is pleased with. He, glory be to Him, loves to be obeyed, loves to bestow blessings, to be kind and generous. Even if He decrees disobedience and wills to withhold, obedience is more beloved to Him, and giving and bestowing are more esteemed by Him. So attributing both kinds of good to Him and both kinds of evil to the self is more appropriate. For this reason the knowers among His servants adopted this etiquette: they attributed blessings and goods to Him, and attributed evils to their place of origin, as the leader of the upright monotheists (hunafa') said: ﴿He who created me, it is He who guides me, and He who feeds me and gives me drink, and when I am ill, it is He who cures me﴾. He attributed the illness to himself and the cure to his Lord. Al-Khidr said: ﴿As for the boat, it belonged to poor people who worked on the sea, so I wished to damage it﴾, then he said: ﴿As for the wall, it belonged to two orphan boys in the city, and beneath it was a treasure belonging to them, and their father was righteous. So your Lord intended that they should reach their maturity and extract their treasure﴾. The believing jinn said: ﴿And we do not know whether evil is intended for those on earth, or whether their Lord intends for them guidance﴾.

The fifth difference: the good deed is attributed to Him because He bestowed it in every respect and from every standpoint, as has been mentioned. There is no aspect of it that does not necessitate its attribution to Him. As for evil, He, glory be to Him, decreed and ordained it only for His wisdom, and in terms of that wisdom it is part of His beneficence. The Lord, glory be to Him, never does evil at all, just as He is not described by it, nor named by it. Rather, all His actions are good, beneficial and wise, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿In Your hand is all good﴾, and the one most knowledgeable of Him said: "And evil is not attributed to You." So He does not create pure evil in every respect. Rather, everything He creates contains benefit and wisdom, even if some part of it is partial and relative evil. As for absolute, total evil in every respect, He, exalted is He, is far above it, and it is not attributed to Him.

The sixth difference: the good deeds that a person performs are existent matters, linked to the will of the Lord, His decree, His mercy and His wisdom. They are not non-existent matters attributed to other than God. Rather, they are all existent matters, and every existent thing is originated, and God is its originator and creator. This is because good deeds are either the performance of what is commanded or the abstention from what is forbidden, and abstention is an existent matter. A person's abstaining from what he was forbidden, his knowledge that it is a vile sin and a cause of punishment, his hatred and aversion to it, and his restraining of himself when he desires it and seeks it, are all existent matters. Likewise, his knowledge of good deeds, such as justice and truthfulness, is a good, and his performance of them is an existent matter. A person is rewarded for abstaining from evil deeds only if he abstains from them out of aversion to them and refrain from them, and restraint of the self from them. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿But God has made faith beloved to you and has adorned it in your hearts, and has made disbelief, wickedness and disobedience hateful to you﴾. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿But as for he who feared the standing before his Lord and restrained the soul from desire﴾, and He said: ﴿Indeed, prayer prohibits immorality and wrongdoing﴾.

In the two Sahihs, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever has three qualities will taste the sweetness of faith: he for whom God and His Messenger are dearer than anything else; he who loves a person only for the sake of God; and he who hates to return to disbelief after God has rescued him from it, as he hates to be thrown into the Fire." The Prophet (ﷺ) made hatred for the sake of God one of the most reliable bonds of faith, and this is the root of abstention. He also made withholding for the sake of God one of the perfections of faith, and this is the root of abstention. He said: "The most reliable bond of faith is loving for the sake of God and hating for the sake of God." And he said: "Whoever loves for God's sake, hates for God's sake, gives for God's sake and withholds for God's sake has perfected his faith." He also made rejecting evil with the heart one of the levels of faith, which is hating it and being averse to it, which necessarily entails abstaining from it. So abstention is part of faith only through this aversion, hatred, refraining and withholding for God's sake. Likewise, the disavowal of Abraham and his people from the polytheists and their deities was not mere abstention, but abstention arising from hatred, enmity and aversion. These are existent matters, a servitude of the heart, from which the limbs' abstention from action follows, just as assent, intention and love for obedience are a servitude of the heart, from which their effects follow in the limbs. This love and hatred are the realisation of the testimony that there is no god but God. It is the affirmation of the heart's worship of God and its love for Him, and the negation of its worship of other than Him and its aversion to it. It is not sufficient for a person to worship God, love Him, rely upon Him, turn to Him, fear Him and hope in Him, until he also abandons the worship of others, reliance upon them, turning to them, and fear and hope in them, and hates that. All of these are existent matters, and they are the good deeds for which God rewards. As for the mere absence of evil deeds, without knowing that they are evil, without hating them in his heart, and restraining himself from them, but rather abstaining because they do not occur to his heart, he is not rewarded for this abstention. In his case, evil deeds are in the same position as they are for a child or a sleeper. However, one may be rewarded for believing in the prohibition of evil deeds even when he has no inclination toward them at all. Abstention is of three kinds: one kind is rewarded; one kind is punished; and one kind is neither rewarded nor punished. The first is the abstention of one who knows that a thing is forbidden and restrains himself from it for God's sake, while being able to do it. The second is like the abstention of one who refrains from it for other than God, not for God's sake. He is punished for abstaining for other than God, just as he is punished for doing it for other than God, for that abstention and withholding is an action of the heart, and if it is directed to other than God, he deserves punishment.
