Did ascending to heaven ever remove anyone from servitude in any way?

And if you make him a god because the prophets called him god, lord, master, and the like, then many of the names of God, Mighty and Majestic, have continued to be applied to others among all nations and in all the books. The Romans, the Persians, the Indians, the Syriacs, the Hebrews, the Copts, and others have continued to call their kings gods and lords.

And in the first book of the Torah: that the sons of God entered upon the daughters of men, saw them to be exceedingly beautiful, and married them.

And in the second book of the Torah, the story of the exodus from Egypt: "I have made you a god to Pharaoh." And in Psalm eighty-two: "God stands in the assembly of the gods."

This is in Hebrew. As for the one who transmitted it into Syriac, he altered it, and said: "God stands in the assembly of the angels." And in this psalm, addressing a people with the Spirit, he said: "I have supposed that you are gods and that you are all sons of God." And God has named His servant "king" just as He named Himself by that.

And He named His prophet "compassionate and merciful" just as He named Himself by that, and He named him "mighty" and named Himself likewise. The name "Lord" (rabb) is applied to other than God, Exalted, in the language of the nation of monotheism, as one says: "He is the lord of the house, the lord of the dwelling, the lord of the camels, the lord of this goods."

Isaiah has said: "The ox knows the one who owns it, and the donkey the stall of its lord, but Israel does not know," meaning those who created them.

And if you make him a god because he made from clay the likeness of a bird, that is, the form of a bird, then he breathed into it, and it became flesh and blood and a real bird, and none does this except God.

It is said: "Then make Moses son of 'Imran the god of gods, for he cast down a staff and it became a great serpent, then he took it in his hand and it became a staff as it was."

And if you say: "We made him a god on the testimony of the prophets, the messengers, concerning him," Ezra said, when Bukhtnasr (Nebuchadnezzar) took them captive to the land of Babylon for four hundred and eighty-two years: "The Messiah will come and deliver the peoples and the nations." And when this period ended, the Messiah came, and who is able to deliver the nations and peoples except the perfect God? It is said to you: "Then make all the messengers gods, for they delivered the nations from disbelief and polytheism, and delivered them from the Fire by the permission of God alone."

And there is no doubt that the Messiah delivered whoever believed in him and followed him from the humiliation of the world and the punishment of the Hereafter, just as Moses delivered the Children of Israel from Pharaoh and his people, and delivered them by faith in God and the Last Day from the punishment of the Fire in the Hereafter.

And God, Glorified and Exalted, delivered through Muhammad (ﷺ), son of 'Abd Allah, His servant and messenger, from the nations and peoples what no other prophet delivered. So if divinity is due to Jesus for this, then Moses and Muhammad are more worthy of it than he is.

And if you say: "We made divinity due to him for the statement of the prophet Jeremiah concerning his birth: 'And in that time (a son will arise to David), who is the light of day, who will reign as king, establish truth and justice in the land, deliver whoever believes in him from the Jews, from the Children of Israel, and from others, and Bayt al-Maqdis will remain without an equal, and he will be called God.'"

It has already been established that the name "God" in the earlier books and others has been applied to others, and it is in the position of "Lord," "Master," and "Father." And if Jesus were God, he would be too exalted to be said: "He will be called God," and he would have said: "I am God," for God, Glorified and Exalted, is not known by such a thing. In this proof by which you made him a god is the greatest evidence that he is a servant, and that he is the son of man, for it says: "A son will arise to David," so this one who arose for David is the one who was named "God." It is known that this name belongs to a created, made, begotten thing, not to the Lord of the worlds and Creator of the heavens and the earths.

And if you say: "We made him a god on the basis of the statement of the prophet Isaiah: 'Say to Zion: rejoice and be glad, for God will come and deliver the peoples, and deliver whoever believes in Him, and deliver the city of Bayt al-Maqdis, and God will display His pure arm there before all the scattered nations, and He will make them one nation, and all the people of the earth will see God's deliverance, for He walks with them and before them, and the God of Israel will gather them.'"

It is said to you: This first requires that it be known that this is in the prophecy of Isaiah with this wording, without alteration of its wording and without error in translation, and this is not known.

And even if that is established, there is no proof in it that he is a perfect God, and that he is uncreated and not made, for it is similar to what is in the Torah of His saying: "God came from Mount Sinai, and shone forth from Seir, and was manifested from the mountains of Paran." There is nothing in this indicating that Moses and Muhammad are two gods.

What is meant is the coming of His religion, His Book, His law, His guidance, and His light.

As for his saying: "God displays His pure arm before all the scattered nations," the Torah has the like of this, and more eloquent than it, in more than one place.

As for his saying: "All the people of the earth will see God's deliverance, for He walks with them and before them," He said in the Torah in the fifth book to the Children of Israel: "Do not fear them, nor be afraid of them, for God your Lord is the one who walks before you, and He fights on your behalf."

And in another place Moses said: "This people is Your people." He said: "I will go before you."

He said: "If you do not go before us, then do not bring us up from here. And how shall I and this people know that I have found favor in Your sight, except by Your going with us?"

And in the fourth book: "If you bring these up by Your power, they will say to the people of the earth who heard from you: God is among these people; they see Him eye to eye, and Your cloud stands over them, and a cloud goes before them by day and becomes fire by night."

And in the Torah also God says to Moses: "I come to you in the thickness of the cloud, so that the people may hear My speaking to you."

In the divine Books and the words of the prophets there is much of this. And what the seal of the prophets related from his Lord, Exalted, that He said: "My servant continues to draw near to Me with voluntary acts until I love him. When I love him, I am his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he grasps, and his foot with which he walks. By Me he hears, by Me he grasps, and by Me he walks."

And if you say: "We made him a god because of the statement of Zechariah concerning his prophecy: 'Rejoice, O daughter of Zion, for I come to you and dwell within you, and I will appear, and many nations will believe in God on that day, and they will be one people for Him, and He will dwell among them, and they will know that I am God, the Mighty, dwelling in you, and God will take the kingdom on that day from Judah, and He will rule over them forever.'"

It is said to you: If divinity is due to him by this, then it is due to Abraham and other prophets, for according to the People of the Book, and you are with them, God manifested Himself to Abraham, revealed Himself to him, and appeared to him.

As for his saying: "I will dwell within you," God, Glorified and Exalted, did not intend the dwelling of His Essence, which the heavens and the earth could not contain, in Bayt al-Maqdis. How could His Essence dwell in a place where He would be subdued and overcome along with the worst of creation? How, when He said: "They will know that I am God, the Mighty, dwelling in you"? Do you think they knew His might by seizing Him, binding His hands with ropes, tying Him to the wood of the cross, driving nails into His hands and feet, placing a crown of thorns on His head, while He cried out for help and was not helped? The Messiah did not enter Bayt al-Maqdis except as one overcome, subdued, and humbled in most of his circumstances.

And even if the coming of these words were established as sound beyond refutation, and their translation were correct as they have claimed, its meaning would be that the knowledge of God, faith in Him, His remembrance, His religion, and His law dwelt in that place. When the religion of the Messiah appeared in it after his raising, there came to be in it faith in God and knowledge of Him that had not been there before.

The summary of the matter: the earlier prophecies and the divine Books did not utter a single letter that requires that the son of man be a perfect God, a true God, uncreated and not made or nurtured. Rather, they did not single him out except with what his brother, and the one closest to him, Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah (ﷺ), was singled out with, in His saying: "He is the servant of God and His messenger, and His word which He cast to Mary, and a spirit from Him."

The earlier prophetic Books and all the prophecies agree with what Muhammad (ﷺ) reported, and all of that confirms one another. And all that the Trinitarians, worshippers of the cross, use as evidence for the divinity of the Messiah from wording and expressions in the Books, these are shared between the Messiah and others, such as his being called a son, a word, the Spirit of truth, and a god. Likewise, he is the Holy Spirit (Ruh al-Qudus). As for the Holy Spirit, it is the secret of God and His command, and it has occurred in the divine Books for other than the Messiah.

It has been applied to several meanings, among them Gabriel, among them the Greatest Name of God, and among them revelation. It has been applied to the Messiah because his spirit did not mix with a drop of semen. "The Holy" (al-Quddus) is the pure, and for this reason "the Spirit of God" was applied to the Messiah. This idafah (construct) is an idafah of honor, like His saying: "the House of God" and "the she-camel of God." Just as the earlier nations used to call themselves "sons of God." Among them is the Qur'an, which is more general than the Qur'an revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ), encompassing every revealed Book.

And as for the Spirit by which there is life, it is the soul (nafs), according to the principle of the Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah, the orthodox majority). It is a subtle body that resembles perceptible bodies, it is created, and it is taken up to heaven with joy. It does not die and does not perish. It is among the things that have a beginning but no end, like Paradise and Hell. Bodies at the Resurrection have two eyes and two hands, and they have a pleasant or foul smell according to their place. The soul is either blessed or punished, and that is the clearest proof that it is created.

The Messiah was called the Spirit of Allah because he possessed a spirit and was brought into being without a part of a living being with a spirit, like a drop of semen separated from a living father. He was originated by Allah's invention alone, and His power is pure.

He was called the Word of Allah because he came into being by His word and command, without an intermediary father or a drop of semen. This is clear.

Likewise, what has been said about the indwelling of the Holy Spirit (ruh al-qudus) in him, and the manifestation of the Lord in him or in his place, has been uttered. Groups among those who ascribe themselves to Islam have fallen into the likeness of the polytheism and disbelief of the others, and what settles in the hearts of the knowers (al-'arifin) of faith in Him, of knowing Him, of His light and His guidance, became confused for them. They thought that this was the very essence of the Lord's Being. Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿And to Him belongs the highest likeness in the heavens and the earth; and He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾. This refers to what is in the hearts of the angels, His prophets, and His believing servants of faith in Him, knowledge of Him, love of Him, reverence for Him and glorification of Him. It is similar to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if they believe in the like of that which you have believed, then they are guided﴾, and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He is Allah in the heavens and in the earth. He knows your secret and your open, and He knows what you earn﴾,

and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He is the One who is God in the heaven and God on the earth. And He is the Wise, the Knowing﴾.

So the friends of Allah know Him and love Him, and they exalt Him above being said to be what is in their hearts. What is meant is the love of Him, the knowledge of Him, and the highest likeness in their hearts, not the very essence of His Being. This is an expression that people commonly use in their speech and discourse. A person says to another: "You are in my heart, and you have never left my eye," just as the poet said:

"And, strange as it is, I yearn for them,
and I ask about them of whomever I meet, though they are with me.
My eye seeks them, though they are in its very pupil,
and my heart longs for them, though they are between my ribs."

And another said:

"Your image is in my eye, and your remembrance is in my mouth,
and your abode is in my eye, so where can you be absent?"

And another said on the same theme, and excelled:

"If I say you are absent, my heart does not believe me,
since you are within it. May my soul be your ransom; you have not been absent.
Or if I say you are not absent, my eye says that is a lie,
so I am bewildered between truth and falsehood."

And another said (on the same theme, in a single line):

"I yearn for him, while he dwells in my heart.
How strange it is for one to yearn for his own heart!"

And whoever has a coarse nature, and whose understanding is veiled from grasping the like of this, it will not be difficult for him to understand from the wording of books that the Essence of Allah, Glorified is He, indwells the human form, unites with it and mingles with it. Exalted is Allah far above what they say.

If you say: "We ascribe divinity to him from the saying of Isaiah: 'It is one of the wonders that the Lord of the angels will be born of humans.'"

It is said to you: That itself requires the soundness of the statement attributed to Isaiah, that it was not distorted in transmission from one translation to another, and that it is a statement disconnected from what precedes and follows it. It is a warning and a proof that he is created and made, and that he is a son of man who is born of man, not of the One, the Eternal Refuge, who did not beget and was not begotten, and to whom no one is equal.

If you say: "We have made him a god from the saying of Matthew in the Gospel: 'The Son of Man will send out his angels, and they will gather all the kings and cast them into the furnace of fire.'"

It is said: This is like the previous one. It did not intend that the Messiah is the Lord of lords, nor that he is the creator of the angels. What testifies to this, and that the pronoun in "his angels" refers to Allah and not to the Messiah, is the statement of Mark in his Gospel in this same place and on this same meaning: "For the Son of Man will disgrace him when he comes in his sanctuary and with his holy angels." So understand this.

It is possible that Allah makes the Messiah an envoy between Him and some of the angels of punishment, with respect to all the kings of disbelief from among those who ascribe themselves to His religion, from the plains of the Resurrection, and bringing them into the Fire.

The pronoun in "the angels" refers to Allah and not to the Messiah. The people are simply ignorant of the station of Lordship and the station of the angels, and of the Arabic tongue into which their language was translated. "And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide." Far be it from Allah that He should be described as the Lord of the angels in that sense. Rather, this is among the most shameful lies and fabrications. Indeed, the Lord of the angels commanded them to protect the Messiah and support him, by the testimony of the Prophet who said among them: "Allah commands His angels concerning you, that they may protect you." Then by the testimony of Luke: "Allah sent to him an angel from heaven to strengthen him."

This is what the Books have spoken, but the liars distorted this concerning Allah and His Messiah, and attributed to the prophets that they said: "He is the Lord of the angels."

When the Gospel testifies, and the prophets and messengers agree, that Allah commands His angels concerning the Messiah to protect him, it is known that the angels and the Messiah are servants of Allah, submissive to His command. They are not lords or gods.

The Messiah said to his disciples: "Whoever receives you has received me, and whoever receives me has received the One who sent me."

The Messiah also said to his disciples: "Whoever denies me before people, I will deny him before the angels."

He said to the one who struck (with a sword) at the high priest's servant: "Put your sword back in its place. Do you not think that I cannot call upon my Father, and He would provide me with more than twelve legions of angels?"

Would one who is the Lord of the angels, their God and their Creator, say this?

And if you ascribe divinity to him by what you have quoted from Isaiah: "A rod shall come out of the stump of Jesse (the house of a prophet), and a branch shall grow out of it. The Spirit of God shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and the fear of God. By him they believe, and in him they trust, and for them there will be the crown and honor forever and ever."

It is said to you: This statement, after the demand that its transmission from Isaiah be proven authentic, and that its translation into Arabic be sound, and that the translations have not distorted it, is an argument against the Trinitarians, the worshippers of the Cross, not for them. It does not indicate that the Messiah is the Creator of the heavens and the earth. Rather, it indicates what the Qur'an indicated, that the Messiah was strengthened with the Holy Spirit. For he said: "And the Spirit of God shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and the fear of God." He did not say: "The life of God shall rest upon him," let alone that God would indwell him and unite with him, and take his humanity as a veil. This Spirit is with the prophets and the truthful (al-siddiqin), and in the Torah (Tawrah) they have: "Those who worked in the Tent of Meeting, the spirit of wisdom and the spirit of understanding and knowledge indwelt them." This is what brings guidance, victory and support.

As for his saying "the Spirit of God," it does not indicate that it is His attribute, let alone that it is God Himself. Gabriel is called the Spirit of God, and the Messiah's name is the Spirit of God.

Whatever is attributed to Allah, if it is an entity existing by itself, is an attribution of a possession to its owner, like "the House of Allah," "the she-camel of Allah," and "the Spirit of Allah." It does not mean a house in which He dwells, nor a she-camel He rides, nor a spirit subsisting in Him. Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿Those are the ones in whose hearts He has written faith and whom He has supported with a spirit from Himself﴾, and He the Exalted has said: ﴿And thus We have revealed to you a spirit from Our command﴾.

So this is the Spirit with which He supported His believing servants.

As for his saying "and by him they believe, and in him they trust," it refers to Allah the Exalted, not to the rod that grows out of the house of prophethood.

Allah has combined these two principles in: ﴿Say: He is the Most Merciful; we have believed in Him, and upon Him we have relied﴾.

And Moses said: ﴿O my people, if you have believed in Allah, then rely upon Him, if you are Muslims﴾.

This is frequent in the Qur'an. He has informed us that Allah supported him with the spirit of knowledge and the fear of Allah, combining knowledge and awe, which are the two principles that the Qur'an combined in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾.

And in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I am the most knowing of you about Allah, and the most fearful of Him."

This is the state of a pure servant. As for the true God, the Lord of the worlds, no fear or awe reaches Him, and He does not worship other than Himself. The Messiah was standing in the performance of acts of worship to Allah in the most perfect manner.

If you ascribe divinity to him by the saying of Isaiah: "A child has been born to us, and a son has been given to us, and the government shall be upon his shoulders, and his name shall be called: Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace..." Wait, and his name shall be called: "Great King, Mighty God, Ruler, Prince, strong in peace in all generations, and his dominion is complete and has no end."

It is said to you: There is nothing in this good tidings that indicates that it refers to the Messiah in any way.

Even if it referred to the Messiah, it would not support what they seek. As for the first point: its indication of Muhammad ibn Abd Allah is clearer than its indication of the Messiah, for he is the one whose government is upon his shoulder and between his shoulders, in two respects. First, the seal of prophethood was on part of his shoulders; it is one of the signs of prophethood foretold by the prophets, and the mark of the sealing of their register. For this reason it was on his back. Second, he was sent with the sword that he carried on his shoulder, and he raised it when he struck with it over his shoulder. The saying "a ruler, ruling, strong in peace" also indicates him. This is the description of Muhammad (ﷺ), the one supported, victorious, empowered, the ruler of peace, for his religion is Islam, and whoever follows him is safe from the humiliation of this world and the punishment of the Hereafter, and from the domination of his enemy over him.

The Messiah was not empowered over his enemies as Muhammad (ﷺ) was. Rather, his enemies were empowered over him, overpowering him, until they did to him what they did, according to the Trinitarians, the worshippers of the Cross. Where then is the correspondence of these attributes to the Messiah in any respect? They correspond to Muhammad ibn Abd Allah (ﷺ) in every respect, and his dominion is complete and has no end until the end of time.

If it is said: "You do not call Muhammad a god; rather, according to you he is a pure servant?"

It is said: Yes, by Allah, he is indeed a pure servant. Servanthood is the most exalted of his ranks. The name "god" came through translations, and what is meant by it is the lord who is obeyed, who has no god, the one worshipped, the Creator, the Provider.

If you ascribe divinity to him from the saying of Isaiah, as you claim: "Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel." And Immanuel is a Hebrew word whose meaning in Arabic is: "God is with us."

Then the Prophet has testified that he is a god.

It is said to you, after the establishment of this statement and its explanation: It does not indicate that the virgin bore the Lord of the worlds and the Creator of the heavens and the earths. For he said: "She shall bear a son," and this is evidence that he is a prophet among the prophets, not the Lord of the worlds.

As for his saying "and his name shall be called Immanuel," it only indicates that he is called by this name, just as people name their sons with kinds of attributes, names, actions and phrases composed of two nouns or a noun and a verb. Many of the People of the Book name their children Immanuel.

Some of your scholars say that the virgin here refers to someone other than Mary, and they mention a story to that effect. What supports this is that the Messiah is not known by the name Immanuel, even if that was his name. That he is called "God is with us," or "God is my sufficiency," or "God alone," and similar expressions, does not indicate that he is a god.

Some of the Trinitarians, the worshippers of the Cross, have distorted this word and said: "Its meaning is: God is with us." Some of their scholars who were fair, and who let their reason govern their desires, rebutted them, and Allah guided him to the truth and gave him sight from his blindness. He said: (Is this the one who says, "I am the Lord, and there is no god besides Me, and I give life and cause death, and I create and provide?" Or is he the one who says to God: "You are the true God alone, who sent Yusu' (Jesus) the Messiah?")

He said: The first is false, and the second is what the Gospel bears witness to. It is obligatory to affirm the Gospel and to deny whoever claims that the Messiah is a god to be worshipped.

He said: The Messiah is not singled out by this name. Rather, "Immanuel" is a name by which Christians and Jews name their children. He said: This exists in our own age, and the meaning of this naming among them is one of noble status.

He said: Likewise the Syriac people name their children "Immanuel," and Muslims and others say to a man, "God is with you." When a man is named with the saying "God is with you" or "God is with us," this is a seeking of blessing through the meaning of this name.

And if you make divinity binding for him on the basis of the words of Habakkuk, which he related from him: "Indeed God, on earth, appears in disguise, mingles with the people, and walks among them."

And Jeremiah also says after this: "God appears on earth and moves about among mankind." It is said to you: this comes after the need to establish first the existence of these two persons, and the establishment of this transmission from them, and the matching of the translation without distortion. These are three stations that are difficult for you to prove. They do not indicate that the Messiah is the creator of the heavens and the earth, and that he is a true god who is neither created nor made. In the Torah there is something of this kind, and more eloquent, and that does not indicate that Moses is a god, nor that he is outside the whole category of the servants of God.

His saying "appears in disguise" is like "God manifested Himself, appeared, and revealed Himself," and similar expressions from the Torah and other divine books.

It is mentioned in the Torah that God, exalted is He, manifested Himself and appeared in disguise to Abraham and others of the prophets, and that did not indicate divinity for any of them. People in their customs and their address have always said: "So-and-so is with us, and he is among us, and he has not died," when his deeds, his sunnah, his conduct, and his bequests are among them and are being practiced among them.

Likewise a speaker says to one whose father has died: "The one who left behind someone like you has not died, and I am your father." And when they see a scholar's student teaching his knowledge, they say: "This is so-and-so in the name of his teacher," just as it was said of Ikrimah: "This is Ibn Abbas," and of Abu Hamid: "This is al-Shafi'i."

And when a king sends a deputy to stand in his place in a city, people say: "The king has come, has judged, and the king has decreed."

And in the authentic divine hadith: God, Mighty and Majestic, says on the Day of Resurrection: "My servant, I was sick and you did not visit Me." It will be said: "O Lord, how could I visit You when You are the Lord of the worlds?" He will say: "Did you not know that My servant so-and-so was sick and you did not visit him? Had you visited him, you would have found Me with him. My servant, I was hungry and you did not feed Me." He will say: "O Lord, how could I feed You when You are the Lord of the worlds?" He will say: "Did not My servant so-and-so ask you for food and you did not feed him? Had you fed him, you would have found that with Me. My servant, I asked you for drink and you did not give Me to drink." He will say: "O Lord, how could I give You drink when You are the Lord of the worlds?" He will say: "My servant so-and-so became thirsty and asked you for water, and you did not give him water. Had you given him water, you would have found that with Me."

And more eloquent than this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed those who pledge allegiance to you, they are only pledging allegiance to God; the hand of God is above their hands﴾, and of this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed God﴾. So if the Muslims were to make lawful what you have made lawful, their argument from this that Muhammad is a god of the same kind as your argument would be no different from yours!

And if you make divinity binding for him on the basis of his saying in the third book of the Kings: "And now, O Lord, God of Israel, let Your word to David come true, for it is right that it be a sign: God will dwell with men on earth. Hear, O peoples, all of you, and let the earth and all who are in it listen. The Lord will be a witness against them, and He will come out of His place, descend, and tread upon the heights of the earth concerning the sin of the children of Jacob."

It is said to you: this book first needs to be established, that the one who spoke it was a prophet, that this is his wording, and that the translation matches it, and that is not known. Beyond that, the discussion of this speech is like the discussion of its counterparts that you have mentioned and what you have not mentioned, and there is nothing in this speech that indicates that the Messiah is the creator of the heavens and the earth, as if he were a god who is neither made nor created. As for His saying: "God will dwell with men on earth," it is like His being with them. When His light, His guidance, His religion, and His prophet are on earth, that is His dwelling. It does not mean that He Himself, in His holy essence, descends from His throne and dwells with the people of the earth. And even if one were to assume the impossible, that this were the case, it would not follow that He is the Messiah, for the messengers and prophets dwelt before him and after him. So what makes the Messiah the God, to the exclusion of his brother messengers? Is it because of the power and authority he had while on earth? Yet you yourselves say that he was seized, and was subjected to the utmost humiliation, abasement and subjugation. Is this the fruit of his dwelling on earth with his creation?

And if you say: his dwelling on earth with his creation is his manifestation in the humanity of the Messiah, it is said to you: as for the manifestation that is possible and rational, namely the manifestation of His love, His knowledge, His religion and His word, there is no difference in this between the humanity of the Messiah and the humanity of the rest of the prophets and messengers, and in this wording, on this interpretation, there is nothing that indicates its being specific to the humanity of the Messiah.

As for the impossible manifestation, which intellects, natures, laws and all prophethoods reject, namely the manifestation of the essence of the Lord in the humanity of a created being from among His creatures, and its union with him, its mixing and its blending, this is impossible both rationally and legally. No prophethood could ever express it at all. Rather, the prophethoods from the first to the last agree upon principles:

The first: that God, glorified and exalted, is eternal, one, having no partner in His dominion, no equal, no opposite, no minister, no counselor, no helper, and no intercessor except after His permission.

The second: that He has no father, no son, no peer, no kinsman in any respect, and no wife.

The third: that He is self-sufficient in His essence, so He neither eats nor drinks, nor needs anything that His creatures need in any respect.

The fourth: that He does not change, and no afflictions befall Him, such as old age, sickness, drowsiness, sleep, forgetfulness, regret, fear, worry, grief, and the like.

The fifth: that He does not resemble any of His creatures; rather, "there is nothing like unto Him," neither in His essence nor in His attributes.

The sixth: that He does not inhere in any of His creatures, nor does any of them inhere in His essence; rather, He is distinct from His creation in His essence, and creation is distinct from Him.

The seventh: that He is greater than everything, greater than everything, above everything, dominant over everything, and nothing is above Him whatsoever.

The eighth: that He is capable of everything, so nothing that He wills can overpower Him; rather, He is the doer of what He wills.

The ninth: that He is all-knowing of everything; He knows the secret and what is more hidden; He knows what has been, what will be, and what has not been, how it would be if it were. Not a leaf falls but He knows it, nor a grain in the darknesses of the earth, nor anything moist or dry, still or moving, but He knows it as it truly is.

The tenth: that He is All-Hearing, All-Seeing; He hears the clamor of voices in the variety of languages, in the diversity of needs, and sees the crawling of the black ant on the bare rock in the dark night. His hearing encompasses all that is heard, His sight all that is seen, His knowledge all that is known, His power all that is within capability; His will prevails over all created beings, His mercy embraces all creatures, and His Footstool encompasses the earth and the heavens.

The eleventh: that He is the Witness who never absents Himself, and who does not appoint anyone to manage His dominion, nor does He need anyone to convey to Him the needs of His servants, or to help Him with them, or to incline Him toward them and seek their mercy for them.

The twelfth: that He is the Everlasting, the Abiding, who does not perish, does not vanish, is not annihilated, and does not die.

The thirteenth: that He is the Speaker, who addresses, who commands and forbids, the Speaker of truth, the Guide to the path, the Sender of messengers, the Revealer of books, and the One who watches over every soul for what it has earned of good and evil; He rewards the doer of good for his goodness, and the doer of evil for his evil.

The fourteenth: that He is true in His promise and His report, for none is truer in speech, none truer in discourse, and He does not break His appointment.

The fifteenth: that He, exalted is He, is Self-Sufficient (Samad) in all the meanings of self-sufficiency, so whatever contradicts His self-sufficiency is impossible for Him.

The sixteenth: that He is Holy (Quddus), Peace (Salam), so He is free from every defect, deficiency and blemish.

The seventeenth: that He is the Perfect, to whom belongs absolute perfection in every respect.

The eighteenth: that He is the Just, who does not oppress nor wrong, and whose servants do not fear any injustice from Him.

This is what all the books and messengers agree upon, and it is among the decisive matters (muhkam) such that no law may come with its opposite, nor may any prophet report its opposite at all.

Yet the Trinitarians, the worshippers of the Cross, abandoned all of this, and held fast to the ambiguous (mutashabih) meanings and the unclear (mujmal) wordings, and to the sayings of those who had gone astray before, who led many astray and strayed from the right way.

The principles and doctrine of the Trinitarians concerning the Lord of the worlds oppose all of this in the strongest opposition and are utterly at variance with it.

Section: That if Muhammad ibn Abdullah ﷺ had not appeared, the prophethood of all the prophets would have been void. The appearance of his prophethood is confirmation of their testimony and a testimony to them of truthfulness. His being sent is among the signs of the prophets before him. God, glorified and exalted, has pointed to this very meaning in His saying: ﴿Nay, he came with the truth and confirmed the messengers﴾.

For the messengers gave good tidings of him and announced his coming, so his coming is itself the truth of their report. It is as if his coming were a confirmation of them, since it is the fulfilment of what they reported. There is no contradiction between this and the other view, that his confirmation of the messengers is by his testimony to their truthfulness and his belief in them: he confirmed them by his word and by his coming, and bore witness to their truthfulness by his very coming and by his word. Similar to this is the saying of the Messiah: ﴿confirming what is before me of the Torah, and giving good tidings of a Messenger who will come after me, whose name is Ahmad﴾.

For when the Torah gave good tidings of him and of his prophethood, his very appearance became a confirmation of it. Then he gave good tidings of a messenger who would come after him, so the appearance of the messenger announced was a confirmation of him, just as his appearance was a confirmation of the Torah. The custom of God with His messengers is that the earlier announces the later, and the later confirms the earlier. So if Muhammad ibn Abdullah ﷺ had not appeared, and had not been sent, the prophethood of the prophets before him would have been void.

God, glorified and exalted, does not break His promise nor does His report lie. He had given good tidings to Abraham and Hagar with clear announcements, and we have not seen them fulfilled, nor did they become manifest except through the appearance of the Messenger of God ﷺ. Hagar was given tidings of a kind that no woman of the worlds was given, except Mary daughter of Imran with the Messiah, though Mary was given tidings of him only once, while Hagar was given tidings of Ishmael twice, and Abraham was given tidings of him many times.

Then God, glorified and exalted, mentioned Hagar, and after her death, as one addressing her through the tongues of the prophets, peace be upon them. In the Torah it is said that God said to Abraham: "I have answered your prayer concerning Ishmael, and blessed him, and multiplied him, and magnified him exceedingly. He will beget twelve great ones." Thus is the translation of some translators.

As for the translation which the seventy-two rabbis of the Jewish rabbis translated, it says: "He will beget twelve nations of the nations." And in it: When Hagar fled from Sarai, an angel of God appeared to her and said: "Hagar, maidservant of Sarai, where have you come from, and where are you going?" She said: "I have fled from my mistress." The angel said to her:

ارْجِعِي إلى سَيِّدَتِكِ واخْضَعِي لَها، فَإنِّي سَأُكَثِّرُ ذُرِّيَّتَكِ وزَرْعَكِ حَتّى لا يُحْصَوْنَ كَثْرَةً، ها أنْتِ تَحْبَلِينَ وتَلِدِينَ ابْنًا تُسَمِّيهِ إسْماعِيلَ، لِأنَّ اللَّهَ قَدْ سَمِعَ تَذَلُّلَكِ وخُضُوعَكِ وخُشُوعَكِ، وهو يَكُونُ عَيْنَ النّاسِ، وتَكُونُ يَدُهُ فَوْقَ الجَمِيعِ مَبْسُوطَةً إلَيْهِ بِالخُضُوعِ، ويَكُونُ مَسْكَنُهُ عَلى تُخُومِ جَمِيعِ إخْوَتِهِ.

("Return to your mistress and submit to her; I will greatly multiply your descendants and your seed, so that they cannot be counted for multitude. Behold, you are with child and will bear a son, and you shall call his name Ishmael, because the Lord has heard your affliction and your submission and your humility. He will be a wild man; his hand will be against everyone, and everyone's hand against him, and he will dwell in the presence of all his brothers.")

وَفِي مَوْضِعٍ آخَرَ قِصَّةُ إسْكانِها وابْنِها إسْماعِيلَ في بَرِّيَّةِ فارانَ، وفِيها: فَقالَ المَلَكُ: يا هاجَرُ لِيَفْرَحْ رَوْعُكِ. فَقَدْ سَمِعَ اللَّهُ تَعالى صَوْتَ الصَّبِيِّ، قُومِي فاحْمِلِيهِ وتَمَسَّكِي بِهِ، فَإنَّ اللَّهَ تَعالى جاعِلُهُ لِأُمَّةٍ عَظِيمَةٍ، وأنَّ اللَّهَ تَعالى فَتَحَ عَلَيْها فَإذا بِئْرُ ماءٍ فَذَهَبَتْ ومَلَأتِ المَزادَةَ مِنهُ، وسَقَتِ الصَّبِيَّ مِنهُ، وكانَ اللَّهُ مَعَها ومَعَ الصَّبِيِّ حَتّى تَرَبّى، وكانَ مَسْكَنُهُ في بَرِّيَّةِ فارانَ.

(In another place is the account of their dwelling, and of her son Ishmael, in the wilderness of Paran, and in it: the angel said, "O Hagar, let your fear be relieved, for God the Exalted has heard the voice of the boy. Arise, lift him up and hold him fast, for God the Exalted will make him a great nation." And God the Exalted opened her eyes, and behold, a well of water; so she went and filled the water-skin from it and gave the boy to drink. God was with her and with the boy until he grew up, and his dwelling was in the wilderness of Paran.)

فَهَذِهِ أرْبَعُ بِشاراتٍ خالِصَةٍ لِأُمِّ إسْماعِيلَ، نَزَلَتِ اثْنَتانِ مِنها عَلى إبْراهِيمَ واثْنَتانِ عَلى هاجَرَ. وفي التَّوْراةِ (التوراة: الكتاب المنزل على موسى عليه السلام، بحسب ما يُعرف بين أهل الكتاب) بِشاراتٌ أُخْرى بِإسْماعِيلَ ووَلَدِهِ وأنَّهم أُمَّةٌ عَظِيمَةٌ جِدًّا، وأنَّ نُجُومَ السَّماءِ تُحْصى ولا يُحْصَوْنَ، وهَذِهِ البِشارَةُ إنَّما تَمَّتْ بِظُهُورِ مُحَمَّدِ بْنِ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ (ﷺ) وأُمَّتِهِ. وإنَّ بَنِي إسْحاقَ كانُوا لَمْ يَزالُوا مَطْرُودِينَ مُشَرَّدِينَ خَوَلًا لِلْفَراعِنَةِ والقِبْطِ حَتّى أنْقَذَهُمُ اللَّهُ بِنَبِيِّهِ وكَلِيمِهِ مُوسى بْنِ عِمْرانَ، وأوْرَثَهم أرْضَ الشّامِ، فَكانَتْ كُرْسِيَّ مَمْلَكَتِهِمْ، ثُمَّ سَلَبَهم ذَلِكَ وقَطَّعَهم في الأرْضِ أُمَمًا مَسْلُوبًا عِزُّهم ومُلْكُهُمْ، قَدْ أخَذَتْهم سُيُوفُ السُّودانِ، وعَلَتْهم أعْلاجُ الحُمْرانِ حَتّى ظَهَرَتْ تِلْكَ البِشاراتُ بَعْدَ دَهْرٍ طَوِيلٍ وعَلَتْ وانْتَشَرَتْ في آفاقِ الدُّنْيا، ومُدَّتْ وعَلَتْ بَنُو إسْماعِيلَ عَلى مَن حَوْلَهم فَهَشَّمُوهم هَشْمًا، وطَحَنُوهم طِحْنًا، وانْتَشَرُوا في آفاقِ الدُّنْيا، ومَدَّتِ الأُمَمُ أيْدِيَهم إلَيْهِمْ بِالذُّلِّ والخُضُوعِ، وعَلَوْهم عُلُوَّ الثُّرَيّا فِيما بَيْنَ الهِنْدِ والحَبَشَةِ والسُّوسِ الأقْصى وبِلادِ التُّرْكِ والصَّقالِبَةِ والخَزَرِ، ومَلَكُوا ما بَيْنَ الخافِقَيْنِ وحَيْثُ مُلْتَقى أمْواجِ البَحْرَيْنِ. وظَهَرَ ذِكْرُ إبْراهِيمَ عَلى ألْسِنَةِ الأُمَمِ، فَلَيْسَ صَبِيٌّ مِن بَعْدِ ظُهُورِ النَّبِيِّ (ﷺ) ولا امْرَأةٌ ولا حُرٌّ ولا عَبْدٌ ولا ذَكَرٌ ولا أُنْثى إلّا وهو يَعْرِفُ إبْراهِيمَ والِدَ إسْماعِيلَ.

(The Torah's (al-Tawrah: the scripture revealed to Moses, peace be upon him, as known among the People of the Book) other tidings concerning Ishmael and his offspring are that they would be a very great nation, and that they would be as countless as the stars of heaven. This tiding was fulfilled only with the appearance of Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah (ﷺ) and his community. The children of Isaac remained driven out, scattered, and enslaved to the Pharaohs and the Copts until God rescued them through His prophet and interlocutor Moses ibn 'Imran, and gave them the land of Syria as an inheritance, and it became the seat of their kingdom. Then He stripped them of that and scattered them over the earth as nations whose honour and dominion were taken away, seized by the swords of the Sudan and subjugated by the uncouth foreigners of the Ḥumrān, until those tidings appeared after a long age, rose high, and spread through the horizons of the world. The sons of Ishmael extended and rose above those around them, crushing them completely and grinding them down, and they spread through the horizons of the world. The nations extended their hands to them in submission and humility, and they rose above them like the rising of the Pleiades, between India, Abyssinia, the far Sus, the lands of the Turks, the Slavs and the Khazars, and they ruled everything between the two horizons and where the waves of the two seas meet. The mention of Abraham became current on the tongues of the nations, so that no child, woman, free man, slave, male or female, after the appearance of the Prophet (ﷺ), fails to know Abraham, the father of Ishmael.)

وَأمّا النَّصْرانِيَّةُ وإنْ كانَتْ قَدْ ظَهَرَتْ في أُمَمٍ كَثِيرَةٍ جَلِيلَةٍ، فَإنَّهُ لَمْ يَكُنْ لَهم في مَحَلِّ إسْماعِيلَ وأُمِّهِ هاجَرَ سُلْطانٌ ظاهِرٌ ولا عِزٌّ قاهِرٌ ألْبَتَّةَ، ولا صارَتْ أيْدِي هَذِهِ الأُمَّةِ فَوْقَ أيْدِي الجَمِيعِ، ولا امْتَدَّتْ إلَيْهِمْ أيْدِي الأُمَمُ بِالخُضُوعِ، وكَذَلِكَ سائِرُ ما تَقَدَّمَ مِنَ البِشاراتِ، ويُفِيدُ مَجْمُوعُها العِلْمَ القَطْعِيَّ بِأنَّ المُرادَ بِها مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ (ﷺ) وعَلى أُمَّتِهِ. فَإنَّهُ لَوْ لَمْ يَقَعْ تَأْوِيلُها بِظُهُورِهِ (ﷺ) لَبَطَلَتِ النُّبُوّاتُ.

(As for Christianity, although it spread among many great nations, the place of Ishmael and his mother Hagar never had any manifest authority or overpowering might at all, nor did the hands of this community come to be above the hands of all, nor did the nations extend their hands to them in submission. The same is true of all the tidings mentioned earlier, and their collective meaning yields certain knowledge that what is intended by them is Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah (ﷺ) and his community. For if their fulfilment had not come about through his appearance (ﷺ), the prophecies would have been null.)

وَلِهَذا لَمّا عَلِمَ الكُفّارُ مِن أهْلِ الكِتابِ أنَّهُ لا يُمْكِنُ الإيمانُ بِالأنْبِياءِ المُتَقَدِّمِينَ إلّا بِالإيمانِ بِالنَّبِيِّ (ﷺ) الَّذِي بُشِّرُوا بِهِ، قالُوا: نَحْنُ في انْتِظارِهِ ولَمْ يَجِئْ بَعْدُ.

(Therefore, when the disbelievers among the People of the Book knew that it is not possible to believe in the earlier prophets without believing in the Prophet (ﷺ) whose coming they were given good news of, they said: "We are awaiting him, and he has not yet come.")

وَلَمّا عَلِمَ بَعْضُ الغُلاةِ في كُفْرِهِ وتَكْذِيبِهِ مِنهم أنَّ هَذا النَّبِيَّ في ولَدِ إسْماعِيلَ أنْكَرُوا أنْ يَكُونَ لِإبْراهِيمَ ابْنٌ اسْمُهُ إسْماعِيلُ، وأنَّ هَذا لَمْ يَخْلُقْهُ اللَّهُ تَعالى.

(And when some of the extremists among them in disbelief and denial knew that this Prophet was from the offspring of Ishmael, they denied that Abraham had a son named Ishmael, and that God the Exalted had created him.)

وَلا يَكْثُرُ عَلى أُمَّةِ البَهْتِ وإخْوانِ القُرُودِ وقَتَلَةِ الأنْبِياءِ مِثْلُ ذَلِكَ، كَما لَمْ يَكْثُرْ عَلى المُثَلِّثَةِ وعُبّادِ الصَّلِيبِ الَّذِينَ سَبُّوا رَبَّ العالَمِينَ أعْظَمَ مِسَبَّةٍ أنْ يَطْعَنُوا في دِينِنا، ويَنْتَقِصُوا نَبِيَّنا (ﷺ).

(Such a thing is not too much for the people of slander, the brothers of apes, and the killers of the prophets, just as it was not too much for the Trinitarians and the worshippers of the Cross, who revile the Lord of the worlds with the greatest reviling, that they should attack our religion and belittle our Prophet (ﷺ).)

[Chapter on his guidance ﷺ regarding the prohibition of seeking cure through forbidden things]

Section on his guidance ﷺ regarding the prohibition of seeking cure through forbidden things

Abu Dawud related in his Sunan from the hadith of Abu al-Darda', may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed Allah sent down the disease and the cure, and He made for every disease a cure. So seek treatment, but do not seek treatment with what is forbidden."

Al-Bukhari mentioned in his Sahih from Ibn Mas'ud: "Indeed Allah has not made your cure in that which He has forbidden to you."

In the Sunan [it is related] from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade the foul medicine."

In Sahih Muslim, from Tariq ibn Suwayd al-Ju'fi, that he asked the Prophet ﷺ about wine, and he forbade him, or disliked that he make it. He said: "I make it only for medicine." He said: "It is not a medicine, but it is a disease."

In the Sunan it is [related] that he ﷺ was asked about wine being put into medicine, and he said: "It is a disease and it is not a medicine."

Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi related it.

And in Sahih Muslim: "From Tariq ibn Suwayd al-Hadrami who said: I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, in our land there are grapes which we press, and we drink from them.' He said: 'No.' I returned to him and said: 'We seek healing for the sick with it.' He said: 'Indeed that is not a cure, but it is a disease.'"

In the Sunan of al-Nasa'i: "That a physician mentioned a frog in a medicine in the presence of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he forbade him from killing it."

It is also mentioned from him ﷺ that he said: "Whoever treats himself with wine, may Allah not cure him."

Treating with forbidden things is ugly by reason and by the Law. As for the Law, it is what we have mentioned from these hadiths and others. As for reason, it is that Allah, glory be to Him, forbade it only because of its impurity, for He did not forbid good things to this Ummah as a punishment for it, as He forbade them to the Children of Israel by His saying: ﴿For the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We forbade them good things which had been lawful for them﴾ [al-Nisa': 160]. Rather, He forbade to this Ummah what He forbade because of its impurity, and His prohibiting it is a protection for them and a safeguard against consuming it. Therefore it is not fitting that it be sought as a cure for diseases and ailments, for although it may have an effect in removing them, it leads to a sickness greater than it in the heart, because of the strength of the impurity within it. So the one who treats himself with it has sought to remove the sickness of the body by means of the sickness of the heart.

Also, its prohibition requires avoiding it and keeping away from it by every means, and taking it as a medicine encourages desire for it and involvement with it, and this is contrary to the intent of the Lawgiver. Moreover, it is a disease, as the Bearer of the Law explicitly stated, so it is not permissible to take it as a medicine.

Also, it imparts to the nature and the spirit the quality of impurity, because the nature is strongly affected by the qualities of medicine; if its quality is impure, the nature acquires impurity from it, how much more so when it is impure in its very essence. For this reason Allah, glory be to Him, forbade His servants impure foods, drinks and garments, because of what they impart to the soul of the state and quality of impurity.

Also, permitting treatment with it, especially when souls incline toward it, is a means to consuming it for desire and pleasure, especially when souls know that it benefits them, removes their ailments and brings their healing; this is the thing most beloved to them. The Lawgiver blocked every possible means to consuming it, and there is no doubt that between blocking the means to consuming it and opening the means to consuming it there is contradiction and conflict.

Also, in this forbidden medicine there are ailments exceeding what is thought of it as cure. Let us suppose the discussion concerns the mother of all abominations, in which Allah has never placed a cure at all, for it is severely harmful to the brain, which is the seat of intellect according to physicians and many jurists and theologians. Hippocrates said in the course of his discussion of acute diseases: "The harm of wine to the head is severe, because it hastens its rising to it, and with its rising rise the humors that are above in the body, and it likewise harms the mind."

The author of al-Kamil said: "The distinctive property of drink is harm to the brain and the nerves." As for other forbidden medicines, they are of two kinds: One of them is that which the soul loathes, and the nature is not roused to assist in repelling the disease through it, like poisons, the flesh of vipers, and other loathsome things. So it remains a burden upon the nature, weighing it down, and then it becomes a disease and not a medicine.

The second is that which the soul does not loathe, such as a drink used by pregnant women, for example. The harm of this exceeds its benefit, and reason requires the prohibition of that. Thus reason and natural disposition agree with the Law in this.

Here there is a subtle secret concerning why the forbidden things are not used for healing. The condition for healing by a medicine is that it be received with acceptance and belief in its benefit, and in the blessing of healing that Allah has placed in it, for the beneficial is the blessed, and the most beneficial of things is the most blessed, and the blessed person wherever he is, is the one who benefits wherever he alights. It is known that the Muslim's belief in the prohibition of this substance is among the things that stand between him and belief in its blessing and benefit, and between his good opinion of it and the acceptance of his nature toward it. Indeed, the greater a servant's faith, the more he dislikes it and the worse his opinion of it, and his nature is most averse to it. So if he consumes it in this state, it becomes a disease for him and not a cure, unless the belief in its impurity, its bad reputation and his aversion to it are replaced by love; and this contradicts faith. So the believer never consumes it except by way of disease. And Allah knows best.
This comparison is with respect to the origin of the revelation, not to its greatness or the excellence of what was revealed.

Chapter: On the levels of guidance, both special and general, and they are ten levels.

The first level: the level of Allah's speaking to His servant while awake, without any intermediary, but directly from Him to him. This is the highest of its levels, as He spoke to Musa ibn 'Imran (may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him and upon our Prophet). Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And Allah spoke to Musa with direct speech.﴾ [An-Nisa: 164]. He mentioned at the beginning of the verse His revelation to Nuh and the prophets after him, then singled out Musa from among them by informing that He spoke to him. This indicates that the speaking that took place with him was more specific than the general revelation mentioned at the beginning of the verse. Then He emphasized it with the true verbal noun (masdar), which is the masdar of kallama, namely taklim (speaking), to remove what the Mu'attilah, the Jahmiyyah, the Mu'tazilah and others suppose, that it was inspiration (ilham), or a sign, or the expression of the inner meaning by something other than speech. So He emphasized it with the verbal noun, which establishes the attribution and removes the suspicion of metaphor. Al-Farra' said: The Arabs call whatever reaches a person "kalam" by whatever way it arrives, but they do not confirm it with the verbal noun. When they confirm it with the verbal noun, it is nothing but the real meaning of speech, like irada (will): one says, "So-and-so willed a willing (iradah)," meaning the real meaning of willing; and one says, "The wall wanted (arada)," but one does not say "iradah," because that is a metaphor, not a reality. This is his statement. Allah the Exalted also said: ﴿And when Musa came at Our appointed time and his Lord spoke to him, he said: My Lord, show me Yourself that I may look upon You﴾ [Al-A'raf: 143]. This speaking is other than the first speaking with which He sent him to Pharaoh. In this second speaking he asked to see [Allah], which he did not ask in the first, and in it he was given the Tablets, and it was by an appointment from Allah to him, whereas the first speaking was not by appointment. In it Allah said to him: ﴿O Musa, I have chosen you above the people by My messages and by My speech﴾ [Al-A'raf: 144], meaning by My speaking to you, according to the consensus of the early scholars (salaf).

Allah the Glorified has informed in His Book that He called him (nada) and conversed with him intimately (najah). Nida' is from a distance and najah is from nearness. The Arabs say: when the circle is large, it is nida', or najah. His father Adam said to him in their dispute: "You are Musa whom Allah chose by His speech and wrote the Torah for you with His own hand?" And likewise the people of the Standing (on the Day of Judgment) say to him when they ask him to intercede with his Lord. Likewise in the hadith of the Night Journey concerning Musa's presence in the sixth or seventh heaven, according to the differing narrations, he said: "That is by His preferring him with the speech of Allah." Had the speaking that took place with him been of the same kind as what took place with other prophets, this specification of him in these hadiths would have no meaning, and he would not have been called "the interlocutor (kalim) of the Most Merciful." Allah the Exalted said: ﴿It is not for a human that Allah should speak to him except by revelation, or from behind a veil, or that He send a messenger and he reveal by His permission what He wills﴾ [Ash-Shura: 51]. So He distinguished between speaking by revelation, speaking by sending a messenger, and speaking from behind a veil.

(Section: Allah's speaking to Musa)

Some of the Ahl al-Sunnah argued against the Mu'tazilah who held that Allah's speaking to Musa (peace be upon him) is metaphorical, by His saying: ﴿And Allah spoke to Musa with direct speech﴾

So He emphasized the verb with the verbal noun, and metaphor is not valid with emphasis.

Al-Suhayli said: I discussed this with our shaykh Abu al-Hasan, and he said: This is good, were it not that Sibawayh permitted in such a case that it be an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) even if it is not described in the wording, so it may be understood as "speaking of some kind," and thus there is no decisive proof in the verse, though the proofs against them are many.

(Revelation and its interpretation)

I say: This is not anything, and the verse is explicit that the intended speaking is more specific than inspiration. He mentioned that He revealed to Nuh and the prophets after him, and this revelation is the general shared speaking. Then He singled out Musa with a specific name and a specific act, which is "kallama taklima," and He removed the suspicion that the general speaking is intended by the verb through emphasizing it with the verbal noun. This indicates Musa's distinction with this speaking. Had the intended meaning been "speaking of some kind," it would have been equal to the revelation mentioned earlier, or less, and that is false. Also, emphasis in this kind of context is explicitly an expression of exaltation and the affirmation of the real meaning of speech and speaking, both verb and noun, and describing it with something that suggests paucity contradicts the context, so reflect on this.

Also, Allah the Glorified said to Musa: ﴿I have chosen you above the people by My messages and by My speech﴾. If the speaking that took place with him were "speaking of some kind," it would not be shared with the rest of the prophets, and there would be no meaning in specifying him with speech. Also, qualifying the verbal noun here indicates its paucity, and that a type of speaking occurred with him, and this is impossible here, for inspiration is a kind of speaking, and that is why Allah called it revelation, and revelation is a kind of speaking. He said: ﴿And We revealed to the mother of Musa: Suckle him﴾ and ﴿And when I revealed to the disciples﴾, and their like.

And 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit said: "The dream of the believer is a speech by which the Lord speaks to His servant in his sleep."

So all these kinds are called "speaking of some kind," but Allah the Glorified singled out Musa and chose him above mankind with His speech to him. Also, when Allah the Glorified mentions Musa, He mentions His speaking to him by the specific name of speaking rather than the general name, as in His saying: ﴿And when Musa came at Our appointed time and his Lord spoke to him, he said: My Lord, show me Yourself that I may look upon You. He said: You will not see Me﴾. Rather, He mentions His speaking to him in a more specific way than that, namely a special speaking, as in His saying: ﴿And We called him from the right side of the mount and brought him near as a confidant (najiyyan)﴾. So He called him (nada) and conversed with him intimately (naja). Nida' and najah are more specific than taklim, for it is a special speaking: nida' is speaking from a distance, which the caller hears, and najah is speaking from nearness. Also, this verse combines elements that prevent interpreting it as Abu al-Hasan said: He mentioned the general revelation, then mentioned the general prophets after Nuh and Muhammad, then mentioned Musa himself after the general mention of the prophets, then mentioned the specific speaking, then emphasized it with the verbal noun. Anyone with even minimal taste for language and the signification of its words will be certain that this context requires that Musa be singled out with a speaking that no one else received, and that it is not "speaking of some kind." So what Abu al-Hasan said is not good, but utterly false. What deceived him is Sibawayh's choice of omitting the description of the verbal noun while intending it; yet Sibawayh did not state this for every verbal noun of this kind, but only said that it is permissible in general. When the speech contains what indicates the intention of emphasis without a description, neither Sibawayh nor anyone else would say that there is an omitted descriptor indicating its paucity, as when one says: "I confirmed the Messenger's truth with confirmation (tasdiq), I believed in him with belief (iman)," or "So-and-so fought alongside the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with fighting (qital), and he helped him with help (nasr), and the Messenger clarified to his community with clarification (tabyin), guided them with guidance (irshad), and gave them guidance (huda)." Would Sibawayh or anyone say that this may be described as "some kind of" belief, clarification, and guidance? The verse is likewise. And Allah the Exalted is the Granter of success to what is right.

Al-Suhayli said: I also asked him about the agent (al-'amil) of the verbal noun when it is an emphasis of the verb, since the emphasized verb does not govern its emphasis, as it is essentially the same in meaning; so what governs it? He was silent for a while and then said: No one has asked me this before you. I think its agent is what would govern it before it if it were a noun, for if it were a noun it would be in the accusative by the implied verb "fa'altu" contained within it. Then I presented his words to myself and reflected on the book, and he had indeed missed what Sibawayh alluded to in the chapter on verbal nouns, rather he stated it explicitly. He made the emphatic verbal noun accusative by a verb that is the emphasis itself in reality, and that verb was omitted, and the verbal noun that is its object took its place, just as "iyyaka wa zaydan" took the place of the governing verb for both. So the estimate becomes: "I struck, I struck a striking," where the second "I struck" is the emphasis in reality, and "striking" has taken its place, being its object. Its governing is only estimated as an absolute object, not as an emphasis. This is the meaning of the statement of the author of the book with additional explanation, and whoever examines it there will find it so. What I now say is the view of Shaykh Abu al-Hasan, because the omitted verb is a meaning, and meanings are not emphasized by themselves, but only by words; and your saying "daraba" is a verb derived from the verbal noun, so it indicates it. It is as if you said: "I did the striking, so I struck," which contains the verbal noun, and therefore you may omit it, as in: "Whoever lies, it is evil for him." You may restrict it with a circumstantial clause, as in: "We stood quickly, so quickly," where "quickly" is a circumstantial clause from the standing. Just as you may restrict it with a circumstantial clause and refer to it by a pronoun, you may also emphasize it with "darban" (striking), as if you said: "striking, striking," or the accusative "darban" containing the explicit "darban," and by it the second governs, meaning "fa'altu," just as that applies to the absolute object when you say: "I struck a severe striking," meaning "I did a severe striking." The emphasis is not like that; it is put in the accusative just as Zayd the second is in the accusative in your saying "I struck Zayd, repeated," which is accusative because it is the first, not because you implied a verb for it. Reflect on this.

[Section: The naming of Jesus as "the Spirit of Allah"]

Two matters remain here.

The first: It may be said: since the breathing (nafkh) into Mary came from the angel, and it is he who breathes souls into all human beings, what is the reason for calling Jesus "the Spirit of Allah"?

And if the souls of all people come into being from this same spirit, what is Jesus's distinguishing characteristic?

The second: It may be said: was the spirit that came to be in Adam, through the breathing of this spirit, the one that was breathed into him by the One who breathed it into Mary by the permission of Allah? Or did the Lord, exalted is He, Himself breathe it, just as He created him with His hand?

It is said: By the life of Allah, these are two important questions. As for the first, the answer is that the spirit breathed into Mary is the spirit attributed to Allah, which He singled out for Himself and ascribed to Himself. It is a spirit specifically distinguished from all other spirits. It is not the angel entrusted with breathing into the wombs of pregnant women, whether believers or disbelievers. Allah, glorified is He, has indeed appointed an angel over the womb who breathes the spirit into the fetus, and records the provision of the child, his term, his deeds, his wretchedness and his happiness.

As for this spirit sent to Mary, it is the Spirit of Allah, whom He chose from among the spirits for Himself. Thus he held the position of a father to the whole species. When his breath entered her womb, that was in the position of the male's impregnation of the female without any intercourse taking place. As for what Adam was singled out for: he was not created like the creation of Jesus from a mother, nor like the creation of the rest of the species from a father and a mother. The spirit breathed into him was not from the angel who breathes the spirit into all his descendants. Had it been so, Adam would have had no distinction by it. Rather, the hadith mentions what he was singled out for over others, and it is four things: Allah created him with His hand, and breathed into him of His spirit. This requires a breather, a breathing, and a source from which the breath was taken. The source from which it was taken is the spirit attributed to Allah, and from it the breath spread into the clay of Adam. Allah, exalted is He, is the One who breathed into his clay from that spirit. This is what the text indicates.

As for whether the breathing was by His direct act, exalted is He, just as He created him with His hand, or whether it occurred by His command, as it occurred with Mary, peace be upon her, this requires evidence. The difference between Allah's creating him with His hand and His breathing into him of His spirit is that the hand is not created, whereas the spirit is created. Creation is one of the acts of the Lord. As for breathing, is it one of His acts subsisting in Him, or is it an effect of His effects subsisting in something other than Him and separate from Him? This is a matter that requires no evidence. This is unlike the breathing into Mary's womb, which is one of His effects, and He attributed it to Himself because it occurred by His permission and command. As for His breathing into Adam, is it an act of His or an effect? In either case, the spirit from which the breath came into Adam is a created spirit, not eternal, and it is the substance of Adam's spirit. So his spirit is even more fitting to be originated and created, and this is what is meant.

If you ask, "What do you make of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If a man dies leaving no child, and he has a sister, then for her is half of what he left﴾, when death is certain?"

I say: the condition is not on death in general, but on a particular kind of death, namely a death without a child.

((Part Five))
